en: Preface to the Abridged Explanation of the *Buddhabhāṣita-Maudgalyāyana-pañcaśata-praśna-sūtra*.
Originally, this two-fascicle scripture encompasses the essentials of the Vinaya school. Its phrasing is clear and manifest, while its underlying meaning is profound and subtle.
It is the pivotal mechanism for beginners entering the Path and the critical juncture for practice during the final age. However, the name of the translator has been lost.

I have doubts as to whether these were not personally proclaimed by the Buddha himself. Alas! Were it not for the great sovereign manifestation of the Lord of the Pea-pods (Śākyamuni), how could the five hundred [disciples] have so easily sought counsel?
Were it not for the supreme sage and profound compassion of Śākyamuni, I fear it would be difficult to repay even half of his kindness.
This is all the more true when one considers that every word in the sutras fully clarifies the points of training (*śikṣāpada*), and every sentence thoroughly expounds the *vinaya*. It must be...
This is that by which the sages and worthies have made their own determinations; it is not something that ordinary people can achieve. What cause for delusion could there be?

One should know that this is precisely the Tathāgata’s extraordinary and wondrous skillful means (*upāya*) for assisting in the revelation of the meaning of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). How can one fail to reflect upon this?

If one stubbornly harbors doubts and refuses to believe, it is the gravest form of slandering the Dharma (*dharmapratikṣepa*), and I fear it will be difficult to escape its consequences. I pray that we may all have deep faith.
Delve deeply. Be careful not to shrink from the multiplicity of its names and characteristics and neglect to study it. You must certainly examine this text thoroughly.

Those who, with a reverent and pure body and mind, rely upon and practice it will likely not lose the essence of the precepts (*śīla-skandha*). Furthermore, they will strictly guard their dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*).

Through the precepts, concentration (*samādhi*) arises; through concentration, wisdom (*prajñā*) is developed. When the three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*) are perfected and radiant, unsurpassed *bodhi* will surely be attained by means of them.
Thus it has been accomplished. However, although the text is clearly manifest, I fear that those of humble learning and beginner’s mind may still not yet be familiar with its underlying purport.
Recently, there have been several commentaries and sub-commentaries; though their wording is largely sufficient, they likewise do not exhaustively detail the meaning.
Therefore, I could not help but provide a further sub-commentary and explanation, titling it the *Lüejie* (Brief Explanation), so as to facilitate future generations and ensure its wide circulation.
There is no interruption. This serves as the preface.
On the Buddha’s birthday, during the middle of the second month in the seventh year of the Chongzhen era, Daoxing Dao Ren respectfully records this at Dao Guo.

A Brief Explanation of the Table of Contents for the *Sūtra on the Five Hundred Matters of Light and Heavy Precepts Spoken by the Buddha in Response to Maudgalyāyana’s Questions*, concerning the offenses committed during these ninety days that pertain to the *Vinaya-ācāra*. (End.
*Sūtra on the Five Hundred Matters of Light and Heavy Precepts Spoken by the Buddha in Response to Maudgalyāyana’s Questions*.
Brief Commentary, Volume One.
Translator’s name lost; appended to the Eastern Jin Records.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Xingzhi, who upholds the broad precepts at Baoguo Temple in Gusu. Narrated.

(△ Now, to explain this sutra, the main text is divided into two parts: first, the explanation of the title; second, the explanation of the text. The explanation of the title has two sections: first, the direct explanation of the title.)

[This sutra] is common to the teachings of five individuals. When it says "spoken by the Buddha," this distinguishes it from being taught by bodhisattvas, celestial immortals (*deva-rṣi*), or manifested persons; rather, it was personally proclaimed from the golden mouth of Śākyamuni Tathāgata. Since it was not spoken by another Buddha, no separate title was established; therefore, it is simply called "spoken by the Buddha. To explain the terms separately:

"Buddha" has the meaning of awakening and illumination. "Awakening" refers to shattering the dense darkness of the great night; "illumination" refers to clarifying the profound depths of the myriad dharmas. This extends to [the meanings of] self-awakening, awakening others, and the perfection of awakening-practice, all of which follow the standard interpretations and are not cited here.

"Spoken" (*śās*) means to gladden (*sāt*). The Buddha employs the eightfold tones of his voice to respond to capacities and treat ailments, thereby bringing joy to the hearts of the assembly; hence, it is called "gladdening. The Sanskrit name *Maudgalyāyana* is translated here as "Clansman of the Mung Beans" (*Cai-shu-shi*). This also follows the standard interpretation. Regarding the Venerable One, he was foremost in supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). [The following is] for the sake of...

The sentiments of sentient beings anticipate that although the living beings of the final age claim to study the Way, they find it difficult to maintain the precepts. Thus, in order to remedy this deficiency when [the teaching] arrives, he raises this question so that our World-Honored One may explain each point clearly, providing people with a ground for progress and cultivation.

This is truly a manifestation of great skillful means (*mahopāya*) in practicing the Bodhisattva path. To prevent wrongdoing and cease evil is called *śīla* (precept); to subdue body and mind is called *vinaya* (discipline). Furthermore, the Mañjuśrī-viśuddha-vinaya-sūtra states: "To subdue affectionate attachment and the dust-laden afflictions is called *vinaya*; because one understands desire, it is called *vinaya*."

Regarding the characteristics of the precepts (*śīla-lakṣaṇa*), their breadth and brevity are summarized by means of five hundred [rules]. As for what constitutes lightness or gravity, this is determined within the five categories (*pañca-varga*) according to their relative weight. For example, the four *pārājika* offenses are grave, while the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses are relatively light; yet among those, the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* are grave [compared to the others in that category].

The *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses are light; down to the *prātideśanīya* offenses, they are heavy; the *saikṣa* rules are light. "Matters" refers to the characteristics of the matters themselves, namely the categories and sub-categories of the five groups of offenses and five hundred rules.

Regarding any offense committed therein, if one encounters a teacher who knows the Vinaya, whether through admonition or formal discipline, or if one recognizes it oneself and performs repentance, and does not commit it again—practicing in this way to harmonize the three karmas and subdue transgressions—is called "right knowledge. This is the ladder for a beginner entering the Path regarding the characteristics of light and heavy matters.

How could one afford to be deficient? Otherwise, they will let their bodies and minds run wild, entirely without restraint; they will be unacquainted with the proper conduct of affairs, deny cause and effect, and regard neither sin nor merit as real. That they thus wander aimlessly and recklessly, inviting calamity upon themselves, is due to this very fault. Alas! Lately, there has been a certain class of arrogant individuals who have left the household life only recently;

they have not yet mastered the scriptures and teachings, nor do they clearly understand the precepts and discipline. They listen to and follow a certain class of wildly unrestrained teachers, claiming attainment for what they have not attained, and as soon as they open their mouths, they say: "I practice the Mahāyāna Sudden Teaching."

To transcend Buddhas and surpass patriarchs, awakening to the Way lies in the mind, not in the outward forms of precepts. What use is such pedantry? It only serves to bind one’s own body. Such criticisms and much talk cannot be fully recounted; it is a pity.

These types of people treat the Vinaya with contempt and disparage the sacred words of the sages. I do not know what kind of mental state or conduct they possess. This is precisely the fault of those who cling to principle while abandoning practice, failing to realize the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena (*li-shi wu-ai*).

In Sanskrit, *Sūtra* means "Scripture. Because it accords with principle and meets the capacity of the listener, it is called a "Scripture" (*Ching-jing*). Furthermore, "Scripture" (*jing*) means "path. Thus, the five categories and five hundred rules below constitute the path for cultivating practice and entering the Way. If one wishes to advance in cultivation by relying on this, beginning from an ordinary person at the stage of vast ground (*po-di fan-fu*), all the way up to—

This is because there is no ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge) that does not enter through this. There are five further layers of profound meaning, including the explanations regarding persons and phenomena, all of which are detailed elsewhere; thus, I shall not labor over the interpretations of others here. Next, regarding the names of the translators: as for those whose names are lost, according to the new commentaries there are several reasons.

Perhaps at that time the imperial court was preoccupied with many affairs and had no leisure to submit petitions; or perhaps the translation work was minimal and their practice of the Way did not endure long before they returned to the West due to circumstances, such that their names were never transmitted here.

As for the translations by Kumārajīva of the Later Qin—such as the *Prajñā*, *Vimalakīrti*, and *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* sūtras, and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and *Śata-dvāra-śāstra*—which greatly propagated the holy teachings, it is said they "belonged to the Eastern Jin. This must certainly be the case. Regarding the division of the Jin into Eastern and Western, it began with Emperor Wu.

The Sima clan received the abdication from Wei and established their capital at Luoyang. When the Western Jin fell into chaos, Emperor Yuan crossed the Yangtze River and re-established the capital in Jiangdong; he ascended the throne at Jiankang, hence it is called the Eastern Jin. Regarding the "Records" (Lù):

some say they are the *Nèidiǎn Lù* (Record of Buddhist Scriptures) by Vinaya Master Xuán of the Tang dynasty. Both await further examination. (△ The first section, the explanation of the title, is concluded. Second, the explanation of the text is divided into three parts: First, the Introductory Section; Second, the Main Body; Third, the Circulation Section. The Introductory Section has two parts. First, the General Introduction, which is further divided into two. First, the establishment of the chapter titles.)

Chapter One: On the Five Categories of Offenses (The "five categories" refers to those explained below, from the *śikṣāpada* up to the *pārājika*. "Category" (*pien*) means a sequential arrangement; it signifies a chapter or section. "Matter" (*shi*) refers to the actual phenomena, namely the five types of cases detailed below.

"Chapter" (*pin*) means a grouping of related meanings; it also signifies a chapter or section. The only difference between these terms is whether they refer to the whole or its parts, and their degree of brevity. (△ Next, entering the text.)

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha. (The phrase "thus" is a term for referring to the Dharma: "I have heard such a Dharma from the Buddha.

It indicates that it was heard directly by myself and is not a fabrication from my own imagination, nor a teaching received through private instruction. The term "at one time" refers to the occasion when teacher and disciple were in accord and the faculties of the student met with the teaching.

The "Buddha" is the Lord of the Dharma, namely Śākyamuni Buddha. As it is the place where the thousand kings reside, it is called Rājagṛha. Regarding "Kalandaka," both the Sūtras and the Vinaya state that it is the name for a mountain mouse. At that time, the King of Vaiśālī had entered the mountains and was sleeping beneath a tree.)

There was a great venomous serpent that intended to come out and harm the king. A mouse on a tree above came down and screeched, waking the king. The king, moved by its kindness, granted it a village for food; thus, this place was named the Kalandaka Village.

In that village there was a very wealthy elder, whom the king subsequently bestowed the title "Kalandaka. Previously, this elder had offered this garden to various non-Buddhist practitioners. Later, upon seeing the Buddha and hearing the profound Dharma, he regretted not having been able to offer the garden to the Tathāgata. At that time, an earth deity, knowing his intention, manifested herself for him.

[The Buddha] caused a calamitous marvel to terrify the various non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), driving them away. He told the elder, "You wish to offer this garden to the Buddha; you should depart at once. The non-Buddhists left full of indignation, while the elder rejoiced. He established a vihāra and went in person to invite the Buddha, who then preached the Dharma therein.

Thus [the words] "Kālaṇa and others departed" indicate that this was the place where the Dharma was preached. However, the audience is missing; it must be understood that the translator omitted it. Furthermore, there are six kinds of accomplishments (*siddhi*) and so forth, which are detailed elsewhere; they will not be explained here at length. (The General Introduction is concluded.
Second, the Specific Introduction is divided into four parts. First, the aspiration and inquiry of the appropriate recipient.)
At that time, Maudgalyāyana rose from his seat and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I now wish to ask a question.

I only pray that the World-Honored One, out of great compassion, will expound it for my sake. (Rising from one's seat to address the teacher is the constant custom between master and disciple. The term "expound" (*yan*) refers to proclaiming and disseminating. This was because the Venerable One asked on behalf of sentient beings.

He first made this formal address before posing his question, as he did not dare to ask abruptly out of respect for the Tathāgata. (△ Second, the Tathāgata praises his goodness and grants permission to ask.)
The Buddha said, “Excellent! That which you have asked can bring great benefit to immeasurable sentient beings. Ask whatever you wish. (‘Excellent’ means ‘capable.

Because of what is asked, there will surely be something explained, so that the multitude may hear and know it, and thereby obtain great benefit. Since this is a question for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, he praises his capability. (△ Third, the actual questioning regarding the offenses committed by the bhikṣus. Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One, as for the bhikṣus of the final age” (this refers distantly to the bhikṣus receiving the precepts in the present time; the meaning of ‘bhikṣu’ is also to be understood as usual. Although it says ‘receiving’ [the precepts]...).

Regarding the precepts: their roots of faith are shallow; they do not revere the Buddha’s teachings nor do they observe the monastic discipline (*vinaya*). Consequently, they treat the Buddha’s words with contempt and violate the *śaikṣa* rules (Sanskrit: *śaikṣakaraṇīya*; Chinese: "that which should be learned"). [In Sanskrit, *duṣkṛta*; Chinese: "wrongdoing" or "ill-spoken"].

While other precepts involve heavy offenses that are easy to maintain, these rules are subtle, difficult to maintain, and easy to violate. One must constantly mindfully train in them; therefore, their specific names as offenses are not listed, but it is simply stated that "one should learn.

Furthermore, they misappropriate the property of the Triple Gem (referring here to the perpetual and guest-monastery assets of the ten directions). They interchange items belonging to one party with those of another, even to the point of encroaching upon or embezzling them. In all such cases, the law of cause and effect is not understood.

[The text] states: "Both are called 'miscellaneous applications' (雜用). Where will one fall? [The questioner] raises these two matters—the miscellaneous applications and so forth—as questions for the assembly. His intention includes the five categories of offenses within; he asks what kind of retribution for transgressions such as these each shall incur.

Maudgalyāyana was not unaware of this, but he requested the Buddha’s answer so that people would develop faith and have no doubts; thus he specifically asked this. (△4. The Tathāgata’s exhortation to listen and permission to speak.)

At that time, the Buddha addressed Maudgalyāyana: "Listen attentively, listen attentively! I shall speak for you. 'Attentive' (di) means reality; 'listening' (ting) means faith. This is the Dharma spoken by the Buddha."

"It is true and without variation. You should cease your discursive thoughts and forget external conditions; listen with sincere faith and reflect upon it well. (△ Second, the Main Body of the Teaching, divided into two parts. First, a general explanation of the five categories to determine the retributive fruits of light and heavy offenses.

Below, a specific explanation of the five hundred rules to correspond to the causes for light and heavy retributive fruits. The first part, the general explanation of the five categories, is divided into five sections. First, the explanation of the retributive fruits of the *śaikṣa* (training) offenses. This follows from the word "speak" mentioned above.)

If a bhikṣu lacks a sense of shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*). (The word "if" is used here as a hypothetical particle; since he is called a bhikṣu, he ought to possess shame and dread of blame. "Shame and dread of blame" refers to clearly understanding cause and effect, being gentle, compliant, and contented.

A sutra says: "There are two kinds of shame and dread of blame: first, shame that one does not commit evil oneself; second, dread of blame that one does not cause others to do so. It further says: "Shame is shame before Heaven; dread of blame is dread of men.

One who possesses shame and dread of blame may be called a human being; if one lacks shame and dread of blame, one is no different from birds and beasts. Even if such a person exists—a man devoid of shame and dread of blame—he would not respect himself, but instead would treat the Buddha’s words with contempt and violate the rules of training for novices.

[One should] wear the three robes and inner garments neatly. ... Furthermore, one should not preach the Dharma to someone holding a parasol. Within these hundred dharmas, if one commits even a single offense and does not repent, one shall fall into hell and undergo great suffering for a certain period of time.

[The following clarifies the duration of the retribution for the offense: The lifespan of the Four Heavenly Kings is five hundred years; yet they fall into hell. (The Four Heavenly Kings dwell in the belly of Mount Sumeru, the place where the sun and moon travel.

They are Dhṛtarāṣṭra in the east, Virūḍhaka in the south, Virūpākṣa in the west, and Vaiśravaṇa in the north. Each has his own domain over which he rules, hence they are called the Four Heavenly Kings. The *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* states: fifty human years...)

One year [of humans] constitutes one day and night for this heaven. In the Sanskrit language it is called *niraya*; here it is translated as "hell" (*diyu*). In total, there are various classifications such as eighteen, thirty-six, and one hundred and eight. In the language of Qin, it is called "Non-existence" (*wuyou*); because there is no joy or pleasure, no flavor, and no delight.

Therefore, it is said that they "do not exist," or "are base," or "have fallen. Because their sense faculties are all destroyed while suspended upside down in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), some say they "do not exist," meaning there is no further place for them to be pardoned.

Those who have committed an offense of the first category fall into the Saṃjīva (Reviving) Hell. This means that those sinners grow iron claws on their hands; as they claw at one another, their flesh falls away. Alternatively, the hell-wardens shout, or a cold wind blows, and they are restored to life. Although the two conditions differ, they are equally revived.

[They remain there] for nine hundred thousand years among humans (the figure should properly be nine million years; the "thousand" is a scribal error). Why? Fifty years among humans constitute one day for this heaven; eighteen thousand years among humans constitute one year for this heaven. [Eighteen...]

Ten thousand years are counted as ten years; one hundred and eight million years are counted as one hundred years. Five hundred times five hundred equals five million; five times eight equals four million; by principle, it should be nine million years—this can be understood.

In this regard, the *Niraya Sūtra*, the *Buddhāhāra Sūtra*, and others each have their own specific quantities, which roughly follow this pattern; therefore, I shall not cite them at length. One should know that for violating even this final, most minor transgression, one still undergoes such long-term suffering—how much more so for the increasingly heavy sufferings that follow!
Should those who study the Way not be cautious? (△ Second, explaining the retribution for the *Pratideśanīya* offenses).

This is an offense of *pāyattika* (a Sanskrit term; in Chinese, this means "confessing to another," so named because it is established based on the object of counteraction). There are four types, such as receiving food with one's own hands when not ill, as clarified in the Vinaya.

This offense must be confessed. It is also called the "method of repentance" (*deśanā*). [The following clarifies the duration: If one were to live for a thousand years in the Heaven of the Thirty-three (*Trāyastriṃśa*), that would constitute one day and night in the hells (*niraya*).

(This is the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. It dwells upon the summit of Mount Sumeru. On each of its four sides there are eight [heavens], totaling thirty-two heavens that surround it. They listen to Śakra’s exposition of the ten wholesome dharmas and take him as their sovereign;

hence it is called the "Thirty-three. The *Śāstra* states: One hundred years in the human realm corresponds to one day and night in heaven. Those who violate this precept fall into the Black Rope Hell and other such sufferings, where their limbs are first measured out with glowing iron cords and subsequently sawn apart.

In human reckoning, this is three hundred and sixty million years. (Regarding the mention of "three hundred million" and so forth for the number of years: there are various types of "billion" (*koṭi*) that differ. There is the billion of one hundred thousand, the billion of one million, and the billion of ten million. If, by...)

Regarding the phrase "ten million as one hundred million," the character for "hundred million" (億) is not an error. The "sixty thousand" (六十千) is a scribal error; the character "ten" (十) should be changed to "thousand" (千). Why? One should know that based on the previous nine million years, when calculated by quadrupling it, the precise total is thirty-six million years.
(△ Third: The Retribution for a *Pāyattika* Offense).

One commits a *pāyattika* (also called *pāyitti*; this means "falling"). One falls into the Saṃghāta Hell. This category consists of ninety rules, beginning with speaking falsely while knowing the truth and ending with [measuring] the Tathāgata’s robes.

The rules concerning the making of robes are abbreviated; the details for both the *naiḥsargika-pāyattikas* and the *pāyattikas* can be understood from the *Bhikṣu-śīla-mūla*. [Below, the time periods are explained: As in the Yāma Heaven, the lifespan is two thousand years.

Falling into hell—(in Sanskrit, *Suyāma*; this means "Good Time Period," or "Exquisite Goodness"; also called *Suyama*, meaning "Time Period," because they sing of joy at that time; or called "Receiving the Objects of the Five Desires")—one's lifespan is as such.

Because of knowing the divisions of time: two hundred human years constitute one day for this deva. Regarding the ten [hells], it is said: "They fall into the hells of Burning, Boiling, and Obstruction. The eight hot hells collectively constitute Burning and Boiling; the eight cold and dark hells collectively constitute Obstruction.
In terms of human reckoning, this is twenty *koṭis* of thousands of years (the calculation of years here should also follow the fourfold multiplication from the second chapter mentioned previously;

this results in a true total of 144 million years. The term "one *koṭi*" here should be understood as ten million. It is evident that the "twenty *koṭis*" mentioned here is also a scribal error). (△ Four: The Retribution for the *sthūlātyaya* Offense).

This constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* (a term of Sanskrit origin). The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: "*Sthūla*" means "great," and "*atyaya*" is a Chinese term meaning "obstruction. Thus, it is a combination of both the Indic and Chinese terms. This indicates that one who commits this offense creates a great obstruction to the path of goodness and falls into the evil destinies.

"Good" refers to the realms of humans and devas; "evil" refers to the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals. Its essence is base and defiled. It is named after its unwholesome nature because it can bring about the offenses of the two categories: the four *pārājikas* and the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣas*. Furthermore, there are two distinctions regarding its ugliness:

for instance, if one commits the two grave offenses of killing or false speech, once completed they constitute a *pārājika*; if one intends to do so but does not complete it, it is termed an "evil *sthūlātyaya*. This applies similarly to the offenses of sexual misconduct and theft.

If one commits a grave offense, it constitutes a *pārājika* upon completion; if one intends to commit it but does not complete it, it is called an "ugly" *sthūlātyaya*. This principle should be applied to the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses as well. For example, in cases such as [the intentional] emission of semen: if completed, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; if not completed, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

The nature of the "ugliness" may likewise be understood. [Below, the time periods are clarified: As for the Tuṣita Heaven, the lifespan is four thousand years. If one falls into hell (Sanskrit: *naraka*; Chinese: *nièlí*), [the duration is calculated accordingly]. (In Sanskrit, *Tuṣita*;

here translated as "Wonderful Fulfillment," or alternatively as *Dǔshìtuó*, here translated as "Contentment," because those within it know contentment regarding the five desires. The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* calls it "Joyful Contentment," meaning that Bodhisattvas in their final birth teach therein and extensively cultivate joy and contentment. The treatise states: "In the human world, four...")

One hundred years [on earth] constitutes one day for this deva. One who commits this offense falls into the Raurava Hell. This is because the hell-wardens seize the person and cast them into an iron cauldron, where they wail and cry out loudly.

By human reckoning, this amounts to fifty billion and sixty thousand years (*pañcāśat-koṭi-ṣaṣṭi-sahasra-varṣa*). (Regarding the figures of fifty billion and so forth herein, they are calculated by multiplying the previous third section by four;

thus, five hundred and seventy-six million years is the actual duration. As for the "five hundred million" (*pañca-koṭi*), the term *koṭi* here refers to ten million. However, "sixty thousand" is a scribal error. (V. Explaining the retribution for the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses.)

This refers to the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (Sanskrit). The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "Saṃgha" means the Saṃgha; "āva" means the beginning, referring to the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of concealment performed before the Saṃgha.

"Śeṣa" means remainder, referring to the formal act of rehabilitation (*āpattivyutthāna*) performed at the end. If one commits this offense, the Saṃgha performs a ritual to remove it; thus, it is named after its objective basis. The *Vinayamātṛkā* states: "Saṃghāvaśeṣa is like a person who has been cut by another, leaving only the throat remaining."

Therefore, it is called "residual" (*śeṣa*). In principle, one must rescue [the offender] early. Those who have committed this offense must urgently repent; this refers to the initial act of stimulating the genitals and emitting semen, continuing until finally having a wicked nature that refuses to accept the admonitions of others.

(Below, the time-periods are clarified: Just as the gods of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (*Nirmāṇarati*) have a lifespan of eight thousand years, so too do those who fall into hell. (They fall into the Great Howling Hell, as explained above. In Sanskrit, *Sudharmā* or *Nimamala*. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: in the language of Qin, it means "Delighting in Emanations," which is the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations.

Because they emanate the five sensory objects themselves and enjoy them, they are called so. Here, "not *kiao*" [means] not being arrogant or negligent; because they emanate their own pleasures, they are free from arrogance and negligence. *Lengyan Jing*... [text continues].

The name "Yan" (Glorious) refers to the Nirmāṇarati Heaven (the Heaven of Delighting in Transformations). Eight hundred human years constitute one day in this heaven. In terms of human reckoning, this amounts to twenty-three billion four hundred million years.

(Regarding the figures for "two hundred thirty" and so forth in this context, one should calculate according to the fourfold multiplication method explained in the preceding fourth fascicle; thus, twenty-three million and four hundred thousand years is the actual figure.

As for the "two hundred" mentioned here in the sutra, it uses the term "billion" (*koṭi*) to mean ten million. It should be understood that "forty thousand" refers to four million years. (△ Six: Explaining the retribution for the *pārājika* offense.)

This constitutes a *pārājika* offense (the four fundamental offenses of sexual misconduct, killing, stealing, and lying). In Sanskrit, *pārājika* is translated by the *Mahāsāṃghika* school as "extreme evil" (*parama-pāpa*). It is also called "abandonment-offense" (*parityāga-āpatti*) or "borderline offense" (*pratyanta-āpatti*). One who commits this offense is forever cast outside the ocean of the Buddha's teachings;

they may not dwell together with the pure assembly of monks. This is like a corpse cast down into the great ocean: the great ocean of the Buddha-dharma does not harbor the corpses of those who have broken the precepts. There are three aspects to this extreme evil: first, retrogression and submergence, because by committing this precept, one has no share in the fruits of the Path;

second, non-cohabitation, for it is not merely that one loses the Path, but that one may no longer dwell together with the two types of Saṃghas—those performing the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) and those performing formal acts (*karmavācanā*); third, falling away, for after casting off this body, one falls into...

Because of the Avīci Hell. The *Caturvarga-vinaya* says: "It is like severing a person's head; they cannot rise again. If one violates this rule, one can no longer fulfill the conduct of a bhikṣu. [The following clarifies the duration of time:

Like the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, where the lifespan is sixteen thousand years, one falls into hell (niraya). This refers to falling into the Saṃjīva (Flaming Heat) Hell. It is said that the hell-wardens place the offenders within an iron city, where flames scorch and rot them.

Because they burn and roast sentient beings, one falls into this hell. In Sanskrit it is called Vāsava-bhūti, or alternatively Pāraṇimitta. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "In the Qin language, it means 'Mastery over Others' Creations. This heaven seizes what others have created and enjoys it for itself."

Because of their pleasure. The *Bie xing shu* (Commentary on the Separate Practice) states: "This is the Heaven at the Peak of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu-śīrṣa*). They achieve their own pleasure by employing the actions of others; this is the Heaven of the Māra King.

One thousand six hundred years among humans constitutes one day and night for this heaven. By human reckoning, this amounts to five hundred twenty-one billion, sixty thousand years. Regarding the figures of "five hundred" and so forth within this [calculation], one should follow the fourfold multiplication explained in the fifth chapter above.

This results in a true total of nine million two hundred and sixteen million years. Furthermore, the term "billion" (*yì*) here should be understood as ten million (*wàn wàn*). The figures such as "five hundred" are also all scribal errors; one should examine this for oneself. Alas, how tragic! Observing it in this light...

Those who practice the Way and receive the precepts must not fail to be cautious. Should they commit even a single transgression, they will undergo such endless suffering as described above. The *Sūtra on the Transformation of Karmic Retribution in the Hell Realms* states:

Bodhisattva Śraddhālakṣaṇa addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, there are currently sentient beings undergoing punishment who are chopped, pounded, and beheaded by the hell-wardens. They are beheaded starting from their feet up to the crown of their heads; once the beheading is finished, a whirlwind blows them back to life, and they are beheaded again. What offense have they committed?"

The Buddha said: "This was caused by [the fact that] in previous lives they violated the precepts during the months of fasting, failed to have faith in the Triple Gem, and were unfilial toward their parents; furthermore, as butchers and executioners, they slaughtered and dismembered sentient beings. Therefore, they have incurred this retribution.

Moreover, within this there are further various sufferings—such as boiling cauldrons, burning furnaces, sword-trees, knife-mountains, freezing ice, and being flayed—which are beyond description. All these are the results of the evil karma they created in life through killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, and drinking alcohol; because they were deluded and lacked a heart of wisdom, they suffered this karmic retribution for their crimes."

The sentient beings addressed the World-Honored One, saying, "By performing what wholesome deeds can one escape this suffering? The Buddha said, "One should diligently practice filial piety toward one's parents; respectfully serve one's teachers and elders; take refuge in and honor the Triple Gem; and diligently practice generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; cultivate loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity;

treat enemies and kin with equality, regarding them as no different from oneself; do not deceive the orphaned or the elderly; do not look down upon those of low station; and protect others as you would yourself. If you are able to practice in this way, you will have repaid the kindness of the Buddhas."

They shall be forever free from all suffering, and shall not fall into the three miserable realms or the eight difficult conditions. In the hells, they shall find rest; their pain shall be stilled and they shall be at peace. Therefore, one should know that suffering and happiness, as well as transgression and merit, do not originally descend from heaven, nor are they produced from the earth, nor are they bestowed by humans.

This is solely what is summoned and brought forth by one’s own mind. Therefore, one should be cautious, reverent, and fearful; be careful not to treat it with negligence. First, one must clearly understand the characteristics of the precepts. Second, one must maintain a single-minded focus, remaining scrupulously pure and free from transgressions, like ice and frost—such is called a person who upholds the precepts with purity.

Take heed. Furthermore, there are five faults in breaking the precepts, as detailed in the *Sifenlü lüejie* (Brief Explanation of the Four-Part Vinaya), which may be consulted later. The above provides a general clarification of the five categories [of offenses], concluding the determination of the retributive fruits of light and heavy sins.

Below, the five hundred [monks] are specifically explained to correspond to the causes for the retributive fruits of light and heavy [karma]. There are sixteen chapters. From the first, the "Chapter on Buddha-Activities" (Buddha-kṛtya), up to the seventeenth, the "Chapter on the Śrāmaṇeras. First, the "Chapter on Buddha-Activities": [The text continues with the narrative of the Buddha’s activities.]
Chapter Two: Inquiry Concerning Buddhist Affairs (*Buddhakārya*). Regarding "Buddhist affairs" (*buddhakārya*):

whether it be the molding or painting of sacred images, the construction of Buddha shrines, or even the paying of homage and making offerings to the Triple Gem—all such acts are termed Buddhist affairs. The term "Buddha-property" mentioned below exists for the sake of these very activities.

Since the Buddha is the most supreme Honored One and these affairs constitute the greatest of undertakings, those who follow and practice them will gain boundless merit, while those who oppose or transgress them will suffer inexhaustible retribution. First, an inquiry is made regarding Buddhist affairs; subsequently, inquiries are made concerning the Dharma, the Sangha, and so forth, in successive order. Generally speaking...
Thirty-Seven Questions and Answers ○ Question on the Transfer of Buddha-Property (First). Question:

(The single character "question" [問] at the beginning of each query refers to the discourse of the Venerable Maudgalyāyana as he questioned the World-Honored One. Suppose Buddha-property was originally located in one place. (As for "Buddha-property," this refers to sculpted or painted Buddha images;

it also includes items such as incense, lamps, banners, canopies, bells, and drums offered before the Buddha in a Buddha-hall or at its original site. If there is a bhikṣu who carries these to another location and makes [them his own],...

Regarding the Buddha’s affairs: what offense is committed? (What crime must necessarily be incurred? Answer: (Every single word of this answer is the speech of the World-Honored One in response to the Venerable Maudgalyāyana’s question.

One commits the *pārājika* offense. (This is the retribution for the extremely grave *pārājika* offense, as explained above in the first section. Here, because one uses a greedy mind for personal gain to transfer this to that, causing mutual presence and absence and resulting in a confusion of cause and effect, it is identical to stealing property belonging to the Buddha;

therefore, one commits the *pārājika* offense. For this reason,) no Buddha-objects whatsoever may be moved. (The term "whatsoever" is a comprehensive statement. The commission of the offense follows the same principle as above; below, an exception is opened: If there is a difficult circumstance, [it may be done].

If the entire community of monks departs—whether due to dangers such as water, fire, swords, kings, or bandits, or if the community is unable to remain—they should inform the assembly. If the assembly grants permission, they may carry the items for Buddhist rites (*buddhakārya*) to another location;

there is no offense. (If the assembly does not grant permission, one commits an offense. Just as one would not dare to move the property of a sovereign human king, it is by principle that the property of the Dharma King must be treated with reverence.)
Therefore, this is not permissible. (Section on Objects and Vessels for Offering, Part Two). Question:

May one purchase offering implements with the remains of materials intended for Buddha objects (referring here to materials left over from the casting or painting of Buddha images) in order to make offerings to the Buddha? Answer: Yes, it may be done.

Since these are all for the Buddha’s enjoyment, they cause the donor to obtain supreme merit. However, if they were used for the worship of deities and the like, it would not be permissible. (Section on Building Halls and Leasing, Part Three).

Question: If a shrine hall is constructed using property belonging to the Buddha, may one pay a fee to lease it? (Leasing refers to what is now called renting or mortgaging. “Property” also refers to items remaining from statues, paintings, and so forth.

If someone constructs a private hall with these items, may they pay a fee to lease it, and having received the payment, use the property for private purposes? Answer: One may purchase all property belonging to the Buddha, but one may not lease it. (This is because the Buddha is not like worldly people who take possession of things. This hall should be used for making offerings to the Buddha.

If the hall is not constructed and there is surplus property belonging to the Buddha, it is permissible to purchase ritual implements with it to offer to the Buddha; however, if one constructs a hall and then leases its use, there is a discrepancy between cause and effect, which constitutes theft.)

The offense regarding property belonging to the Buddha is identical [to that of the Sangha]; it must not be alienated. If someone should wish to purchase this hall, one should accept five times the price as stated in the following text; the proceeds obtained must be used for original Buddhist services (*butsuji*), only then will there be no fault. (Regarding the lending of property belonging to the Buddha, see Question Four).

Question: When a bhikṣu performs Buddhist services—whether in a monastery or at the home of a donor—such as making offerings to the Triple Gem, performing repentance rites, or reciting sutras, these are indeed "Buddhist services" (buddhakārya), even though they are termed "Dharma services.

Once the service is completed, if a donor offers a "Buddha-slave" or similar items as a token of gratitude, may the bhikṣu accept such a Buddha-slave, ox, donkey, or horse? Whether for himself or on behalf of another, may he borrow or employ them? Answer: If he knows that these were originally the property of the Buddha, he must not accept them.

This is because it constitutes the misappropriation of the Buddha’s property. However, if he does not know this, he may accept them. Why? Because they were acquired through improper means [and thus do not belong to the Buddha].

[One incurs an offense] because they do not know at all that this is the property of the Buddha, nor do they know that there is sin in using the offerings of a donor (*dāna*). [However,] if one knows [it is the Buddha's property] and deliberately violates [the rule], one incurs an offense. Regarding "a slave of the Buddha": this refers to one who was purchased with the property of the Buddha or one who is made to perform labor before the Buddha.
(Question 5: Building a Fence on Monastic Land).

Question: If a stūpa is erected on monastic land and a fence is constructed using the property of the Buddha, may the Sangha dwell within that fenced area? (Since it is monastic land and a monastic stūpa, it stands to reason that the Sangha should dwell there; however, as the fence belongs to the Buddha, may the Sangha reside within it? Answer:

If one knows it is the property of the Buddha and enters intentionally, one commits a *pāyattika* offense (as described above, with the retribution of the Saṃghāvaśeṣa). If one does not know, there is no offense.

If one knows and dwells there intentionally—whether after a single admonition by one who knows the Dharma, or even up to three admonitions—one commits a *nihsargika-pāyattika* offense. This is because the offense is determined (*nihsargika*), meaning it is definitively severed and cannot be rectified.

This is termed "decisive judgment. One who commits this offense falls into the Great Howling Hell (Mahāraurava), as described above. If, after four admonitions, one persists in the transgression, it becomes a grave offense, resulting in the same retribution as that of the Reviving Heat Hell (Tapana) and others.

Regarding "admonition" (*kṣepa*): one should say, "Virtuous One, although this is monastic ground and belongs to the Sangha’s stūpa, the enclosure belongs to the thousand Buddhas. To use the property of a Buddha is unwholesome. Do not dwell here; by dwelling on this ground, you incur an offense. First, you disobey the word of the Buddha; second, you subvert cause and effect. This is absolutely impermissible.

In this manner, one should instruct and admonish with a gentle countenance once, twice, and even up to three times, revealing the truth so that the person recognizes their fault and quickly reforms through repentance. Therefore, it is called "admonition. If, despite such admonition, one does not repent or reform, one immediately incurs this offense. This is for the sake of firm and diligent protection.

Even if it were a Buddhist fence, or even a Buddhist stūpa, there would be no offense. [This concludes] the detailed explanation of the *Sifenlü lüejie* (Brief Commentary on the Four-Part Vinaya) regarding the method for repenting *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses. (Thus ends the sixth question concerning the gift of material wealth to the Saṃgha.)

Question: Suppose an old Buddhist hall has collapsed (to collapse is termed "huài"). The current owner rebuilds it using his own private wealth (subsequently, another donor uses their own funds to construct a Buddhist hall).
He then offers the old materials (such as leftover bricks, tiles, timber, and so forth) to a bhikṣu. May the bhikṣu accept them? Answer: No, he may not.

Because it is property belonging to the Buddha, one may not take it; to calculate its value constitutes an offense. Furthermore, it may not be used for other purposes. Ultimately, what should be done? One should simply use it before the Buddha according to one’s means, so as not to waste the merit of those who previously offered it.

Even if it is ten parts decayed or ruined, there may be no fault. The *Saṃgharakṣita Sūtra* says: "In the past, there was a bhikṣu who privately took timber from a dilapidated Buddhist monastery to build his own room. Later, he was reborn in hell, where his karmic retribution manifested as a great pillar that burned him. Be cautious of this! (Question 7: On the Buddha’s Fences and the Sangha’s Land).

Question: If land belonging to the Saṃgha (such as land for monastic cultivation) is used to construct a general enclosure (a perimeter wall for protection), and there are already wells, fruits, and vegetables within that enclosure, may they be eaten?

Answer: They may not. (Regarding the "well," it should be written as "and" [meaning "both"]. Since these are objects belonging to the Buddha used for the construction of the enclosure, they belong to the Buddha; therefore, it is said they may not be eaten. Below, an exception is granted.

If the enclosure was built using the property of a *dānapati* (donor) for the sake of Buddhist services, one must first offer the fruits and vegetables to the Saṃgha before eating them. (After making offerings to the Buddha, [the remainder may be consumed].)

When making offerings to the Saṃgha before the Buddha, it is improper for the Saṃgha to eat first; therefore, one must not eat [before the offering is made]. (Regarding the price used for purchase: what is appropriate?

If one purchases [food] at five times the price—for example, buying food worth one *qián* or five *qián*—this price was originally intended for Buddhist ritual services (*buddhakārya*), so there is no fault. However, if one knows that the item is property belonging to the Buddha, and instead of paying the price to purchase it, one simply eats it oneself, the gravity of the offense depends on the amount of money involved.

By knowing [the status of the object] and willfully violating the rule out of greed for food and stinginess regarding wealth, one incurs guilt. The Vinaya states: "If the value reaches five *qián*, one commits a *pārājika* offense. Here, "five *qián*" refers to one unit of currency in the Western Regions (Xiyu), which corresponds to sixteen units of the local currency here.

One small coin (*kāśa*) is worth eight *wen* of silver; one that calculates to the value of one *qian* of silver constitutes a grave offense (*pārājika*). If it is less than five *qian*, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense, and so forth. Furthermore, it is said that the currency of the Western Regions is not fixed, consisting of both gold coins and silver coins;
I shall not cite further details here. (Question Eight: On Repaying the Buddha’s Debt).
Question: If one owes goods to the Buddha, how should they be repaid? (Should interest be added? Answer: One should repay the principal goods directly. (Why not add to the repayment?

Because the Buddha neither profits from nor incurs losses, no interest is added. (Lending money and charging interest are termed "profit and loss. Nevertheless, [the offender] will enter hell because the causes and effects of misappropriating the Buddha’s property are difficult to escape.

(The following text provides scriptural proof. Formerly, after the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa*—(this must refer to after Kāśyapa’s *nirvāṇa*; *nirvāṇa* is a variant transliteration of *niepan*)—[the following occurred].
There was a bhikṣu who was diligent and intelligent (possessing both practice and understanding).

A certain brāhmaṇa, seeing that the bhikṣu was diligent, intelligent, and virtuous, offered his daughter to the bhikṣu so that she might become a bhikṣuṇī (in order to seek the Dharma of supramundane liberation). The bhikṣu accepted her.
Because the woman was beautiful, the bhikṣu later conceived lustful thoughts and committed an act of impurity (an act of sexual misconduct; the gravity of the offense may be inferred). Together...

He lived [simply], merely managing his business together with his fellow residents. He spent one million coins each on the requisites for the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, and another million on food and clothing.

This bhikṣu was extremely intelligent; because he possessed both practice and understanding, he was able to preach the Dharma and enable others to attain the fruits of the four paths. Since he could thus benefit others, why would he not benefit himself?

Therefore, reflecting upon the gravity of my own offenses—specifically because I had misappropriated the property of the Triple Gem, which made my transgression particularly heavy—I desired to repay this debt. I immediately traveled to the kingdom of Śākya to beg for alms.

He had acquired a great amount of money and intended to repay it. While on the road through the mountains, he was bitten by a "seven-step snake" (*saptapada-vṛścika*)—a term for a venomous serpent that injects its poison as it bites (this occurrence being summoned by his own karma).
Knowing that he would die within seven steps, [the bhikṣu] spoke to his disciple while still six steps away:

"Where shall I repay the goods? Send me back to my native land. (Since there were many places where the debt could be repaid, he asked "where" as a way of entrusting his final instructions. He said to you: [continue as before].
"Once you have repaid the goods, return here; I shall stay here and wait for you. When the disciple had finished repaying the goods, he returned and reported this.

[The master] immediately rose seven paces and died, falling into the Avīci Hell. Upon first entering the Warmth (Uṣṇa), before reaching the Great Heat (Pratāpana), he recognized it himself, thinking it was a warm bathhouse (because he possessed intelligence and discernment).

He then raised a loud voice to chant sūtras, recite hymns, and offer prayers. (The term "bai" refers to *brahman* chanting; it is the same as the eulogies used here in this land. [This occurred] in hell.
Among the various sinners and ghosts there, those who heard the chanting of the sutras were awakened and attained liberation. Thus, several dozen people were saved (and emerged from hell).

The hell-wardens became greatly enraged and raised iron clubs to strike them; they died immediately and were reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. (The following concludes the preceding passage and offers a warning:
By this one may verify that the property of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha must not fail to be repaid. Because of such repayment, even though one undergoes punishment, [the debt is cleared].

Therefore, one may emerge at times [from the hells]. (This implies that if one does not repay [one's debts], it is difficult to leave hell. There are three faults regarding the earth: first, abandoning the path due to greed and committing a grave offense; second, misappropriating the property of the Triple Gem; third, being unable to digest the offerings of the faithful. It is for these reasons that one remains there.
Nevertheless, by relying on the merit of reciting sutras, chanting hymns, and making vows, one is able to reach this point. Without this merit, one would still be unable to escape the evil realms.
Thus, the boundless merit of the Buddha’s name, sutras, and mantras can be seen in this. (The ninth question: Regarding the residual use of dust from stupas).

Question: If one sweeps dust from atop a Buddha-stūpa and discards it, is there an offense? (There are various types of stūpas: a Buddha-stūpa has thirteen tiers; a Pratyekabuddha-stūpa has eleven tiers;

an Arhat-stūpa has four tiers; a Cakravartin has a stūpa but no tiers. This Buddha-stūpa refers to the thirteen-tiered type. According to the Āgama-sūtras, there are three intentions for constructing a stūpa: first, to manifest the person’s supreme dignity; second, to cause others to give rise to faith; third, to repay the Buddha’s kindness.)

Therefore, one should always diligently perform the sweeping and cleaning without negligence. Answer: It may be discarded; it must not be used for other purposes. (Since it has been stated that a Buddhist stūpa is itself the property of the Buddha, one should know that this applies even to minor items; how much more so for those of great value? The Dharma of the Buddha is profound and subtle, reaching such an extent.

To prevent small faults from becoming great and to make people understand cause and effect and the clarity of sin and merit, it is said: "Do not slight small good deeds, thinking they bring no merit. This is precisely what is meant by the saying:
"Though a drop of water is minute, it gradually fills a large vessel. [End of Question Ten: Taking Interest on Property Belonging to the Buddha].

Question: If a bhikṣu takes property belonging to the Buddha and gives it to others, taking its interest for his own use, does he commit an offense? (The term "interest" (*xi*) means "to produce"; it is like lending money in the secular world to seek profit.

Answer: It is of the same substance as the property of the Buddha. (Since the interest exists because of the Buddha's property, they are said to be of the same substance. To use it constitutes) a grave offense in both cases. (Why is this? Because the principal and the interest are combined; (the "interest" is the profit).
Since it was given to the Buddha, there is sin, but no merit. (Why is there no merit? Because he has corrupted the Dharma-body for the sake of [worldly gain].

Because it is a physical form (the property of the Buddha belongs to the *dharmakāya*. As for those who [claim] it is for the sake of the physical form, they greedily seek after the property of the Buddha to nourish their own physical bodies. Alas! Even a bhikṣu’s faithful offerings are feared to be difficult to digest;

how much more so when one uses the property of the Buddha to generate interest and profit? Therefore, it is said that both commit a grave offense. (The Eleventh Question: Asked by the Buddha’s Servant).

Question: If the master of a Buddhist monastery (the term "monastery" [tú] refers here to the image of the Buddha; one who maintains and guards the stūpa or temple is the "master of the monastery") sends a "Buddha-servant" child to attend to a bhikṣu, may the bhikṣu accept this?

Answer: He must not accept it. Why? Because these are the property of the Buddha. These are the pure attendants (*śrāmaṇera*) who sweep the monastery, add incense, change the water, and serve before the Buddha;

thus they are called "Buddha-servants. Therefore, a bhikṣu must not employ them. To use the property of the Buddha arbitrarily constitutes an even more serious offense. The master of the monastery likewise must not grant such service on his own authority. Be careful of this. (Buddha)
The Twelfth Section: On Making Food by Labor. Question:
If a bhikṣu intends to provide food for the Buddha through labor, may he take the property of the Buddha and use it to purchase clothing and food? Answer: He may not. (Why is this?
A bhikṣu is a disciple of the Buddha; even so, there is no principle of performing labor for hire, let alone taking the property of the Buddha to make clothing.

Regarding consumption: if a bhikṣu sees that a Buddhist shrine hall is collapsing or that sacred images are dilapidated, and he possesses the skill to restore them through modeling or painting, he may resolve to do so; provided that he takes only the merit of the work and does not take the profit.

To say that the Buddha performed manual labor would be to categorize him among those such as earthworkers and water-masons who seek profit to sustain their livelihoods; therefore, this is unreasonable. One who contradicts this incurs an offense. (Question 13: On White-Robed Laypeople Eating the Buddha’s Food)

Question: If a layperson (śrāvaka) provides materials for the Buddha—such as property acquired through household labor or wages earned by working for hire—and after completing the work, uses these items to prepare food and invite the Saṃgha, may the monks eat it?
Answer: They may not eat it. [Objection: Since he has already provided for the assembly of monks, why should they not eat it? [Response:

Although it passed through the hands of a layperson, it is still the property of the Buddha. This is the layperson’s means of supporting his family; it is appropriate for him to use it in that manner. However, if it were a bhikṣu, knowing the Dharma yet violating it, he would likewise incur an offense by calculating the value of the money. Therefore, it is said they "may not eat it," not because it is not the Buddha's property.
The author does not comment on this. Examination of the Fourteenth Inquiry: Seeking Profit through Buddhist Services. Question:

If a bhikṣu performs Buddhist services or Dharma services—whether acting as the Buddha’s representative in proselytization or performing recitations for laypeople—is it permissible for him to handle gold, silver, or coins? Answer: It is not permissible to handle them.

If he does so with a mind of greed or arrogance, he commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense (an offense involving forfeiture). (Buddhist services and Dharma services may involve customary worldly expressions of gratitude; however, if one takes money or goods for these, it is akin to usury and trade, and is likewise [prohibited]).

To work as a hired laborer violates the Buddha’s precepts; therefore, it is not permitted. According to the teachings, a bhikṣu should only beg for food and must not possess money or wealth. However, if someone offers a gift for the sake of the Dharma and it cannot be refused, one should transform it into "pure property" (pariśuddha) and apply it toward a separate meritorious deed.
The forfeiture offense (naiḥsargika-pāyattika) is as explained above in the first section regarding the retribution for transgressions. (Question Fifteen: On Donors Cultivating Merit).

Question: If someone offers oxen, donkeys, horses, or slaves to a bhikṣu for the purpose of performing Buddha-related activities—such as carving images of the Buddha and other such Dharma-related tasks, including the printing of scriptures—may the bhikṣu accept them?
Answer: He may accept them and put them to use, but he must not squander them. (According to the sūtras, one must not raise cats, wildcats, dogs, or similar animals.)

Regarding oxen and horses: those permitted to be accepted are only for the sake of complying with the donor’s intention to generate merit; they are merely temporary expedients and not the permanent Dharma. While a person may perhaps remain [as a householder], one who has left home to study the Way must sell such items as oxen and other livestock, for to keep them would wound the heart of compassion.

Fearing that one cannot accommodate many such things, one should also know the proper time for oneself. Bows, swords, and military weapons are absolutely not to be accepted. These are instruments of injury and mutilation, which are certainly inappropriate and violate prohibitions.
Be on guard and do not accept them. (From *The Buddha’s House: Questions on Private Entrustment*, Part Sixteen.)

Question: If someone has donated a dwelling to the Buddha that has not yet been used, and which has never been offered to the Buddha or the bhikṣus, may one temporarily reside there? Answer: One may not.

(Regarding offerings made out of faith to the Buddha: one must not [use them for oneself], as they are the property of the Buddha. To appropriate what belongs to the Buddha also incurs a grave offense. One should daily sweep and clean, waiting until after the offerings to the Buddha have been completed;
only then may one use [the space] as convenient. [End of] Question Seventeen from the *Xùmíng Kěxī*).

Question: If there is a donor who "continues the Buddha’s light"—that is, offers incense and lamps to the Buddha—since the lamp can illuminate places not reached by the sun or moon, it is called "continuing the light.

May it be extinguished during the day? Answer: It must not. If it is extinguished, one commits a *pāyattika* offense. [Objection: The Buddha possesses a constant radiance; fundamentally, there is neither light nor darkness for him. Why, then, would there be an offense? [Reply: Although it is said that the Buddha has no distinction between light and darkness, the donor gains merit.

Therefore, to extinguish the lamp is a transgression. The donor’s original intention in seeking merit is to maintain the flame constantly, day and night. If you intentionally extinguish it, you violate their reverent faith and diminish their merit.
There is no offense. Be careful regarding this (Question 18: Eating, Sleeping, and Sitting Before an Image). Question:

If it is not a Buddha-hall, nor a place where the Buddha regularly resides—such as a monk’s quarters or a meditation cell—but a Buddha image is situated therein, may a bhikṣu eat, drink, sleep, or lie down before that image?
Answer: It is permitted. (The following serves as an illustration: Even when the Buddha was in the world, [disciples] still ate, slept, and lay down before him.

Furthermore, this is not permitted before an image (of the Buddha). Nevertheless, one must remain respectful and must not turn one’s back lightly. As prescribed in the teachings: "Standing before the Buddha, one is not permitted to sit; sitting before the Buddha, one is not permitted to lie down.

If one must lie down, one must provide a screen—using such things as curtains or screens to shield oneself—and must not lie naked or be negligent; being careful and pure, one incurs no fault. If there is the light of a lamp, one must not pass through or remain within the light of one's feet.
This light belongs to the Buddha; to tread upon the Buddha’s light is a transgression and yields no merit. If one has one's own separate lamp, one may [do so]. (Ancient masters...)

I still dare not presume to fathom even the shadow of his hall, let alone the Buddha’s radiance. In all his movements and deportment, he always maintained a sense of reverence and awe, never allowing himself to become negligent or lax, lest he lose his correct wisdom. Entering into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, marvelous and wondrous skillful means are likewise contained therein; the phrasing is plain, yet the meaning is rich and abundant.
This can be seen here (the nineteenth question regarding visiting stupas together). Question:
If a bhikṣu climbs a Buddhist temple, a Buddhist stupa, or a Buddhist wall to look out into the distance, what offense does he commit? (It is like a worldly person climbing high to gaze afar.)

Therefore it is said, "viewing from afar"). Answer: If one does not know [of the prohibition], there is no offense. If there is indeed an urgent or difficult matter, and one ascends, there is likewise no offense. (Difficult matters may include incidents such as fire, water, or weapons).

If one knows [the prohibition] and yet ascends intentionally, one commits an offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). (Regarding the diagrams of stupas and the like: first, these are the property of the Buddha; second, the Buddha images are situated within the tiers. To treat the sages with irreverence incurs guilt; this is inappropriate even for the laity, let alone for a bhikṣu.

An ancient master said: "Do not ascend the grounds of the Triple Gem without cause; do not casually walk through the midst of a stupa. Unless it is to sweep the ground or add scented water, even the merit of a Wheel-Turning King would be lost.")

[If the offense is] light, upon encountering one who knows the Dharma, one should immediately repent with sincerity; by reforming one's faults, it may be cleared. If it exceeds three admonitions and the offense is determined, and exceeds four admonitions, it constitutes a grave offense (pārājika).

[The words of admonition vary according to the specific matter and should be understood by the student. One must be careful not to treat this lightly. (This refers to the twentieth section on "Using the Later to Question the Former").

Question: (If a bhikṣu) uses designated items to produce Buddhist scriptures—such as items donated by a dānapati—and subsequently obtains other items (items later donated by others), may he not use the original items but use only the later ones?
Answer: He may not. Because having consented to the original items, it would then be improper (for him to be greedily insatiable;

there would be a discrepancy between cause and effect; and his words would be untrue). Since these three faults exist, it is not permitted. It does not matter whether they are items belonging to the Buddha or items belonging to the Dharma; it is excellent to use all that is available, for the merit is great. (The Buddha’s private use of silk: Question Twenty-one.)
Question: May a bhikṣu purchase silk for the Buddha to make robes? Answer: He may not; this is a gift of faith intended as an offering before the Buddha, such as banners, canopies, and the like.

They come seeking merit. Yet a bhikṣu, with a covetous mind and without shame, takes it privately; this is precisely the theft of the Buddha’s property. It causes others to lose their resolve for the path and, by principle, constitutes a grave offense. One must guard against this. (The twenty-second question: On the excellence or inferiority of images.)

Question: (If a bhikṣu) fashions the physical form of a Buddha-image, what offense does he commit? Answer: Regarding all Buddha-images, regardless of whether they are beautiful or ugly, one must not fashion their physical forms.

The transgression is extremely grave (resembling a pārājika or a crime of immediate retribution). One must absolutely not do so. (Physical form refers to the appearance and features, such as height, proportions, beauty, or ugliness.)

"All things" refers to gold, silver, copper, wood, and so forth. Now, the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) of a Tathāgata, manifested through the power of compassion, are difficult to fathom. While it may be possible for these marks to appear before [the body] is fully formed, once it is fully formed, such marks are certainly impossible.

Furthermore, regarding one's parents—if they are beautiful or ugly, handsome or plain—can a child inherit their physical appearance? Therefore, one incurs a grave offense. Among the monastics and laypeople today who do not understand the Dharma, this transgression is exceedingly common. Be cautious, be cautious! (Regarding the formation of marks, see Question Twenty-three).
Question: If a person—whether monastic or lay—creates a Buddha image and does not fashion a nostril (perhaps by oversight), may a later person add it? Answer: Yes.

"One cannot [revert]" (the same applies here). Why is it said that one "cannot"? Because it has already been accomplished. It is like a person whose parents have impaired faculties; the child sees this and cannot bear it, yet he can no longer restore them. Therefore, it cannot be done again.
The world abounds in foolish views; therefore, one should exercise restraint. (This concludes the twenty-fourth inquiry concerning leaning objects against a Buddhist wall. Question:
Previously, it was stated that there is an offense for a bhikṣu to climb upon a Buddhist wall. Now, may one lean objects such as a staff or other items against a Buddhist wall? Answer: One must not.

To do so constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (an offense involving forfeiture). (The "wall" mentioned here refers to the walls of a *buddhavihāra* [Buddhist monastery], such as those found in modern temples, where images of the Triple Gem and other figures are painted upon the decorated walls. As for leaning objects against them, this likewise constitutes a minor offense.)
[This constitutes] an offense of arrogance toward the sacred image. (The following text provides scriptural evidence: Once there was a bhikṣu who entered a monastery to pay homage to the Buddha.

A brahmin skilled in reading physiognomy observed this bhikṣu and saw that he possessed the marks of a devaputra’s merit. He then spoke to the bhikṣu, saying: "I have a daughter; I wish to give her in marriage to you, bhikṣu.

You should now together cease the monastic path and return to secular life. The bhikṣu replied: "Wait until I have finished paying homage to the Buddha and returned. One who harbors such thoughts while engaged in [this act] will surely diminish his merit. The bhikṣu...
He then took his *khakkhara* staff, leaned it against the wall of the monastery, entered the temple to pay homage to the Buddha, and then went back out.

The Brahmin no longer spoke with him. The bhikṣu asked for the reason. [The bhikṣu said: "Will you give me your daughter? (He was asking for what he had previously promised. The Brahmin said, "I will not. [The bhikṣu asked: "Why will you not give her?
The Brahmin said, "Just now I saw that the bhikṣu possessed the marks of nobility, so I gave her; now those marks are no longer there."

Therefore, he did not give it. The reason for this was that [giving it] would have exhausted his merit. (First, it would have caused him to become arrogant toward the sages and worthies; second, his intention would have been improper. It should have been thus.)
[Conclusion of the Warning: For this reason, one must not lean objects against the walls of a Buddha hall or the walls of a stūpa.

To do so violates the precepts and causes the destruction of immeasurable merit (as can be seen here among the thirty thousand and eighty thousand minor rules in the Vinaya). An ancient saying goes: "To dye green is easy; to cultivate pure virtue is difficult. If one does not attend to minor details, it will ultimately bring ruin to one's great purpose."
Those who have newly entered the Path should exercise self-restraint. (From *The Questions of Humans and Devas Concerning the Property of the Buddha*, Part 25). Question:
May a bhikṣu fashion images of devas, humans, worldly beings, or animals using the property of the Buddha? Answer: One may fashion them in the presence of the Buddha, but not away from the Buddha.

This is because it is the property of the Buddha. Regarding "devas in the presence of the Buddha," these are Brahmā, Śakra, and others. Regarding "worldly beings," these are such as Anāthapiṇḍada and others. Regarding "animals," these include the Garuḍa and others who, having been transformed by the Buddha, constantly remain beneath his seat, protecting the Dharma and receiving his teachings.
Therefore, there is no fault in performing [the ordination]. (From *Dù bù zhī běn wèn*, Question Twenty-Six). Question:

If a bhikṣu ordains a person without knowing their origins (their lineage and source), and later, after the ordination, discovers they were a slave of the Buddha, yet does not release them, what offense does he commit?

(The two characters "dù hòu" [after ordination] should be read as "hòu dù" [ordain later] for the sake of textual fluency). Answer: To ordain someone while knowing [this] constitutes a grave offense. (This is because a "slave of the Buddha" is, in fact, the property of the Buddha.)

If one did not know [of the offense] previously, it is as it is; once known, one must immediately dismiss [the person]. (If one repents, there is no fault. If one does not dismiss them, one also commits a grave offense. (Because the transgression remains even more severe if one knows and yet does not reform.
If one wishes to save others, one must certainly examine them; one must be cautious regarding this essential point. [This concludes] the second inquiry repeated above, number twenty-seven.)

Question: Is such a person on the Great Path? Answer: No. (The *du ren* bhikṣu violated the Buddha’s prohibitions for that reason; he feared neither cause and effect nor felt shame, and lacked wisdom. Therefore, he is not on the Great Path.

However, as for those who are "slaves of the Buddha," they are those who separately used money to purchase [the right to serve], calling upon them to sweep and perform labor before the Buddha. This is not what is meant by the present title. It refers rather to practitioners who have resolved their minds to attend to the Buddha, undertaking manual labor and exerting physical effort.

Those who study today must be careful not to mistake this and treat it with negligence. If a practitioner acts in this way, they will bring calamity and retribution upon themselves. Why is this? Because all Buddhas of the three periods and the patriarchs of successive generations entered the Way through the gate of practice. Reflect on this. [Regarding] making images to obtain goods: [Note: The text provided contains a fragmentary commentary regarding the improper conduct of certain monks and the correct understanding of service to the Buddha.]
Question (28). Question:

If one possesses private wealth, [one may] generally resolve to create an image; since the person who creates the image is not restricted to being either a monk or a layperson, it says "possessing [private wealth]. [One may then] commission a bhikṣu to fashion the Buddha image.

Question: May the author (the bhikṣu who is capable of acting) take the object? Answer: He may not. (There are two faults here: first, because it was obtained by the Buddha, it is the property of the Buddha; second, since he already possesses this capability...)

It is excellent when both parties perform the task together as a meritorious act. If one takes the goods for oneself, it is equivalent to working as a hired laborer, which violates the essence of a bhikṣu; therefore, it is said that one must not [do so] (Question Twenty-nine: On Buddhist Banners and Buddhist Affairs).
Question: (If there is a gift of faith,) may a bhikṣu take a banner first offered to the Buddha—a banner for making offerings to the Buddha—and use it for Buddhist rites?

(A "banner" [fan] means "to turn"; it turns evil into good, hence it is called a banner. Answer: It may be used for Buddhist rites. (Alternatively, one may use it separately to make canopies or curtains before the Buddha; or hold a small banner to lead the way during the incense procession—these all constitute Buddhist rites.

However, it must not be used for other purposes. This is permissible provided that the donor does not object. Why is this so? Regarding the merit of a banner, if it is moved by the wind even once, one receives the retribution of a Wheel-Turning King.)

This donor is the very foundation for seeking merit; therefore, it is said that if one does not permit [the practice], one shall not obtain [the fruit]. If one permits it, then it is permissible. (From the *Tongli San Shi Wen*, Question Thirty).

Question: Is it permissible to perform prostrations to the seven past Buddhas? Answer: It is permissible. Why? Because their *dharmakāya* is identical. (Within the scriptures themselves, there are both the seven past Buddhas and the seven present Buddhas;

furthermore, they are divided into past and present: Vipaśyin and the others are of the past, while Krakucchanda and the others are of the present. As for saying "it is permissible," although the names and titles of the Buddhas of the three periods differ, their *dharmakāya* is non-dual. Therefore, if one can prostrate with a sincere mind, the merit is boundless.

Since there is no distinction between past and future [in terms of the essence of the Buddha], the meanings of the names of the seven Buddhas are detailed and clear in the *Sifenlü lüeshu* (Brief Explanation of the Four-Part Vinaya). Below, I shall cite... [allowing the third to be treated as one]. Question thirty.
1). Question:

If a person (the donor) first promises three assemblies for the Buddha (the three assemblies being either three occasions for performing Buddha-activities, three locations for the site of practice, or three months, etc.), and then (the bhikṣus combine them) into one assembly (due to stinginess regarding expenses and resources, they consolidate the three into one;
although this does not fulfill the donor’s intention for the three assemblies, it likewise fails to establish the designation of the three sessions). Or three...

Question: Is it permissible to complete the three acts of giving incense (the matters of the three assemblies)? Answer: It is not permissible. (Why? To act contrary to one’s own words constitutes a transgression. (First, greed and stinginess;

second, false speech—one would incur the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. Alas! In this degenerate age, monks have shallow faith and treat Buddhist rites as child’s play. Will they not surely invite various karmic retributions upon themselves? Should they not be cautious!
[This concludes the thirty-second inquiry on Repenting Transgressions and Overstepping Rules].)
