The answer is: "If one receives them while sitting down, it is better to do so at the very beginning. If one does not receive them while sitting down at the beginning, it is also permissible to receive them at the time of departure. (Below, the subsequent [procedure] is clarified...)

One must receive [the *varṣā*] in the place to which one has moved. Once the thirty-nine days are completed, if there is business (meaning there is further business at that location), one may go directly there;

it is not necessary to receive [the *varṣā*] again for another thirty-nine days. If one does not return to the original place, then regardless of where one received the *varṣā*, one may also receive the *varṣā* at that moved location.

Since one can practice meditation there and there must also be a community, it is permissible. This explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "If one cannot obtain... and so forth. This is the general purport of this chapter.
This is specifically for those who encounter difficulties; it opens the way without distinction [and] does not conclude with the question of "not receiving" (the *saptāha-vidhi*).

Question: If a *bhikṣu* travels while neither having formally concluded his seat (*niṣīdana*) nor received the seven-day leave (*saptāha-vidhi*), and thus violates the rules, may he still receive his seniority (*varṣa*)? [Note: Seniority is attained upon the completion of the summer retreat.]

(He asked this as a summary question. He replied: "I do not know the Dharma, yet I have already received the *la* (seniority). Because I knew the Dharma, I acted in opposition [to the rules] and received it; thus I do not obtain the *xia* (summer retreat seniority). (*Xia* is synonymous with *la*.

On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, the monastic seniority is renewed. The sixteenth day marks the year since the Bhikṣu’s birth into the fivefold Dharma-body. Since the Bhikṣu has left secular life, he does not calculate by secular years, but only counts the summer seniority;

that is why it is so. The *Zenghui ji* says: 'La' means 'to join. It refers to the meeting point of the new and the old. This opens the following section: knowing [the rule] yet not obtaining [the status], what is the ultimate result? If one seeks excellence through a single admonition from the assembly during the summer retreat (*xia seng*)—(the *xia seng* refers to the aforementioned..."

Regarding the *laba* (winter retreat) administrator: the monks should offer this admonition: "Virtuous One, if you wish to benefit yourself in accordance with the Dharma, you should enter the formal retreat (*sīmā-bandha*) and receive the Dharma. It is not appropriate to violate the teachings; to violate the teachings is to treat the Buddha’s words with contempt. To treat the Buddha with contempt is unwholesome.

Virtuous One, you should have faith in the Buddha’s words and must not fail to enter the retreat or receive the Dharma. The preceding and following admonitions should all follow this pattern, merely adapting them according to the specific circumstances. Upon receiving such an admonition, one should immediately repent and comply by entering the retreat and receiving the Dharma; this is the proper course.

If one does not comply, nor accepts the entry into retreat or the reception of the Dharma, then one should be admonished a second and a third time. If, after the third admonition, one still does not accept it, one commits an offense of obstinate speech (*pratikṣepaṇīya-śikṣāpada*), which must be formally adjudicated.

(Because they slight the Dharma of the precepts and lose their virtuous practice, if one) repents (and seeks to resume the formal reception), one may obtain it. At the time of receiving it, one must inform the assembly; only then may one receive the formal reception and so forth through repentance.

First, one repents before those who have offered the admonition. As for the announcement, either the admonishing teacher leads it or one repents before the great assembly, making the following announcement. Observing this, the matter of formally binding oneself to the seat and receiving the Dharma is absolutely indispensable.
According to the regulations, once the formal reception is established, one must immediately contemplate the true reception. (Question 19: What is the consequence of not receiving it?)

Question: If a bhikṣu does not perform the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to admonition) at the conclusion of the summer retreat (*varṣā*), what offense does he commit? [The summer retreat is concluded by the *pravāraṇā*; it extinguishes offenses and generates merit; therefore, one must perform the *varṣā-pūrṇa*. This question follows from that premise. Answer:
Suppose a single bhikṣu does not accept the *varṣā-pūrṇa*. The community should admonish him to accept it.

If he accepts after one admonition, up to three admonitions, this is considered "good" (i.e., virtuous). [If he does not, his fault will be set forth below. If he does not accept after more than three admonitions (i.e., upon reaching four admonitions), he commits an offense of definitive judgment (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). If he does not accept after four admonitions...

He is not a śramaṇa (identical to a worldly person). Why? Because he is unwilling to accept the Dharma of the Tathāgata (it should be understood that he incurs a pārājika offense; neither sitting in meditation nor observing the *varṣa* can exempt him.
Since he calls himself a bhikṣu, he should exert himself). [End of the twentieth question regarding the closing of the retreat after midday.]

Question: (Regarding a *bhikṣu*) who has newly received the precepts during the summer retreat—specifically one who arrives last on the day of the ordination and the retreat is formally concluded after midday—is it permissible for him to receive the *varṣā* (the formal end of the rains retreat)?

(This question arises because while the conclusion of the retreat generally occurs at dawn, this case is somewhat different; hence the inquiry. Answer: Yes, he may receive the *varṣā*. However, he may not do so during the final watch of the night (it appears that during the first watch of the night, he would still be permitted).

Regarding those who may not enter later: first, because the day belongs to the next morning; second, because they lack sincere resolve. Therefore, it is said they "may not. This also applies to those who arrive last; there is no distinction in the opening [of the rite] for them. (The twenty-first question on forgetting the reception and being permitted to sit).
Question: (A bhikṣu) has forgotten to receive the seven-day leave (*saptāha-kalpa*) during the summer retreat (*varṣā*). If he goes out once, is he permitted to remain in retreat? Answer: No.

If one remembers [the offense], one may perform the confession (*pratideśanā*). However, within a single sitting, one must not exceed two or three confessions; if one exceeds two or three, the *varṣa* (rainy-season retreat) cannot be completed.

Once confessed, one should not commit the offense again. To commit it again is not called "confession. This is the same as the preceding passage; the analogy cited therein makes this clear. Therefore, it is said that one does not obtain the formal act of confession (*pratideśanā-karman*).
One obtains [the *varṣa*] by speaking according to the specific matter committed. (This concludes the twenty-second question: "Receiving the *varṣa* under a roof").

Question: When a *bhikṣu* is observing the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat), if it rains, may he move to a roofed shelter and still complete the *varṣā* there? Answer: He may indeed complete the *varṣā* according to the Vinaya.

He ought to sit in the open on the *sīmāmaṇḍala* (boundary circle) to manifest the merit of fulfilling the summer retreat; because he has transcended the boundary, moving due to rain does not constitute an obstacle. This is a provisional expedient for such circumstances. (The twenty-third question concerning obstacles to the formal conclusion of the retreat).

Question: (Suppose there is a bhikṣu who), having arrived at a certain location for the rains retreat, has formally entered the retreat; yet, due to some obstacle or impediment, he is unable to proceed [to his intended destination].

[Question: May one perform the *pūrvakāla-sīmā-bandha* (preliminary boundary-binding) from afar [if one is unable to reach the site due to obstacles on the road]? [Answer: No. One may only perform the *paścimakāla-sīmā-bandha* (subsequent boundary-binding) upon reaching that place.
[If one cannot even reach there later,] if there is a monastic residence along the way where one can stay, one should settle there for two or three days to prepare the quarters.

The method of preparation is as explained below; thereafter, one should request the Saṃgha to perform the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation) to receive the thirty [rules].

On the ninth day, one departs. (Upon departing, one should perform the formal ritual for receiving the dharma. Having completed the thirty-nine days of sitting and wishing to depart, one goes directly to that place to fulfill the subsequent sitting and receive the *varṣā* [rain-retreat].

What if there are no monks? How should it be? If there is no monastic residence, five or more persons may together establish a boundary (*sīmā*) and sit. (One must likewise receive the dharma of having completed the thirty-nine days) before sitting.

(If one wishes to go and observe the *varṣā* [rainy season retreat]), one should leave one or two persons to guard the boundary. (However, if one wishes to go,) one may only depart after completing thirty-nine days.

(As for observing the *varṣā*, it is permissible. If a later person (these three characters are likely a scribal error; if) departs before the thirty-nine days are complete (to fulfill the requirement for observing the *varṣā*), the person who departed earlier does not know this.

(Even if there is a fault in being incomplete, the former seat is not lost. One may also observe the *varṣā* there. The later person loses [the merit], for they know that departing before the full number of days constitutes a fault; thus, they have violated the Buddha’s word in departing.

Consequently, one loses the previous seat and may not receive the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) ordination either. Thus, it is known that one must depart only when the full term of days has been completed. This was established as an opening provision for those who were unable to reach the end [of the retreat], and there is no other distinction. (The twenty-fourth inquiry on the *sīmā-bandha* [seating] at the *dāna-kula*).
Question: May one person up to four persons sit in a formal assembly (*niṣīdana*) at the house of a layperson? Answer: No.

Five or more persons may do so (only those numbering five or more may perform the ritual action of *karmavācanā* to establish a small boundary [*kṣudrasīmā*] and sit; if the assembly is smaller than that, it is not in accordance with the Dharma, and thus they may not [sit]. [The twenty-fifth question on the establishment of a sitting by a single person.]

Question: May a single *bhikṣu* sit in formal meditation (*niṣīdana*) in a secluded place? Answer: (One should say: "No. Since even four people or more may not do so, how much less a single person? (This concludes the introductory section.

If a boundary has already been established (*sīmā-bandha*), it need not be re-established. Two or more persons may [do so], but a single person may not. (The character "yi" [以] should be read as "yi" [亦].)

Why is this? Because there is no one with whom to share a seat. (Because there is no companion, it cannot be obtained. There is no boundary; [if there is] only one person or two persons or more, none may obtain it.

(Five persons are required. If one wishes to perform the *prātimokṣa* ceremony in a secluded place, one must further invite monks so that there are five or more people present to establish the boundary (*sīmā*) for the session.

Only then may one observe this practice of sitting in meditation for the annual retreat (*varṣa*). Without establishing the boundary, it is strictly not permitted. Let the student reflect upon this and not neglect it. (The twenty-sixth inquiry regarding offerings made during the session.)
Question: During the summer retreat (*varṣā*), may a bhikṣu accept invitations for alms from others or receive items entrusted to him by others?
May he do so for up to ten days or even three months? Answer: If he accepts with a mind free from greed, there is no fault, regardless of the duration or distance.

If one has a mind of greed, one must relinquish [the robe] within ten days, because the *ātyayika-cīvara* (emergency robe) is specifically permitted for only ten days; this may be understood by examining the Vinaya texts in detail. (Question Twenty-seven: On the performance of conditioned activities).

Question: During the summer retreat (*varṣā*), within the boundary (*sīmā*) of the monastery, one should perform non-conditioned tasks (*asaṃskṛta-karman*). If one performs conditioned tasks (*saṃskṛta-karman*), is it permissible for him to remain seated?

Answer: Regarding meritorious deeds (*puṇya-karman*), he may direct others to perform them. As for other [non-meritorious] matters, he may not. (If there are beneficial tasks such as those for the Triple Gem, he may merely instruct others to do them;

it is not appropriate to engage in them personally, lest his dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*) be impaired and his meditative sitting (*dhyāna*) be interrupted. Regarding those other [tasks] which he may not perform, he incurs the offense of "working for hire" (*karmakara-doṣa*); therefore, this is prescribed. [End of Section on Summer Retreat Repairs, Question Twenty-Eight.]
Question: Regarding those who observe the summer retreat (i.e., bhikṣus), how should they repair a dilapidated dwelling?

Should it be repaired at the beginning of the retreat or when the retreat has concluded? (This question follows upon the preceding discussion regarding what ought to be done. Answer: If it is damaged during the three months [of the retreat], one must repair it immediately (regardless of the specific time).

If there is a monk in charge of affairs, before the *anvāya* (pre-retreat) period, he should make a formal proclamation, saying: "The dwelling is dilapidated; it shall be repaired. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, if a building is leaking, it should be repaired at the end of spring. If it is thatched with grass, one should use [grass] again.
Supplement: If it is covered with tiles, one should likewise repair it with tiles, and so forth. (Question 29: On a Bhikṣuṇī Coming to Receive the *Varṣā* [End-of-Rains] Observance). Question:

When a bhikṣu has completed his summer retreat (*varṣā*) and is receiving the *pravāraṇā* (the invitation for criticism), if a bhikṣuṇī comes within the boundary (*sīmā*) seeking to receive the *pravāraṇā* from the assembly, should she be granted it?

Answer: Two or more bhikṣuṇīs may be granted it. (This is because among the Eight Respectful Precepts for bhikṣuṇīs, they must request the *pravāraṇā*; therefore, they may receive it. One bhikṣuṇī may not. (The following provides the explanation.)

Because of this. (Why? Because a nun alone has crossed the boundary and committed a grave offense. (Due to the nun’s commission of a grave offense, she is not permitted to participate in the *varṣā* [rainy-season retreat]. [The upper section concludes the *varṣā*;
the lower section begins the chapter on "Matters Concerning Ordination"].)

Chapter Six: On Delivering Persons from Worldly Affairs (*Du Ren Shi Pin*). "Deliverance" (*du*) refers to the act of uplifting, rescuing, and liberating. Sentient beings of the Final Age are oppressed by the sufferings of domestic life and are unable to transcend the world. Desiring to leave the household life in order to cross over the great ocean of birth and death, they are said to "deliver.

Having previously established the boundaries for retreat, entered the summer rains retreat, and practiced seated meditation—thereby achieving self-benefit—one must also benefit others; therefore, this follows with the Chapter on Delivering Persons from Worldly Affairs. It contains nine questions and answers. (Question One: On Delivering People as a Solitary Individual).

Question: May one *bhikṣu* ordain a *śrāmaṇera* (by bestowing upon him the ten precepts)? Answer: Two may do so; one may not. Why? Because one serves as the *upādhyāya* and the other acts as the *ācārya* to instruct him.

The *upādhyāya* transmits the dharma of the precepts directly, while the *ācārya* admonishes him regarding the rules of conduct. This was not the case during the Buddha’s lifetime, when even a single person could do so. Therefore, it is more excellent for many to act together.
One who acts alone as a teacher may not ordain others [and must instead inquire at a distance from a second].

Question: (A *bhikṣu*) who ordains a *śrāmaṇera*—is it permissible for him to request a *upādhyāya* (Sanskrit: *upādhyāya*; translated as "Preceptor" [Heshang] in the Kingdom of Khotan, and here meaning "One Who Gives Birth by Power") from afar?

(The "Preceptor" is the *kalyāṇamitra*, the teacher through whose power the powers of the Path of the Three Vehicles and the fivefold *dharmakāya* are all born. Answer: It is not permissible. (Once ordained, he becomes one's primary teacher. Since one has already been ordained, and furthermore because this concerns the timing prescribed by the Vinaya, one may not request a preceptor from afar.

This is because if one were to go elsewhere to request another teacher to come and act in his stead, it would be improper. Why? Because once another has ordained him, that person becomes his disciple. Alternatively, if one were to perform a remote, empty salutation and request, the original recipient remains the primary teacher by name, serving as the witness.)

This is also not permitted. To receive the title in vain without being able to face-to-face transmit the lineage is to improperly usurp the rank of a master; therefore, [the rule] was established: [if one’s] *varṣa* (seniority) is deficient, one may not ordain others (Question Two).

Question: If a *bhikṣu* who has not yet completed five years of seniority (*paṃca-varṣa*) ordains another person, what offense does he commit? Does his disciple obtain the precepts? Answer: If he knowingly ordains [a person] in violation of the Dharma, he commits the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

(However, if he encounters one who knows the Dharma and offers admonition, and subsequently reforms and repents, it is permissible. If he does not cease after three admonitions, he commits the offense of *pārājika*.

(The above answers the question regarding the teacher’s offense; the following answers the questions regarding the disciples, etc. If the disciple did not know that [the teacher’s action] was contrary to the Dharma, and if at the time of receiving [the precepts] they were earnest and sincere—[there is no offense].

One may also receive the precepts through other thoughts. However, if one knows that the teacher is unrighteous, yet possesses other perceptions or volitions, or harbors doubts that are not urgent, then one does not obtain the precepts.

Only when ten years of summer retreats (*varṣa*) are fulfilled may one become an Upādhyāya; only when five years of ordination (*upasaṃpadā*) are completed is one fit to be called an Ācārya. Nevertheless, one with wisdom is permitted to leave the teacher, whereas one without wisdom must remain for the rest of their life. One without wisdom, even if they have completed five or ten years, is still not permitted to act as a teacher and ordain others, let alone those who have not yet reached that duration.

Therefore it is said that they "do not obtain" [the status]. This is a regulation established because rushing leads to failure. (This concludes the fourth inquiry regarding acting as a teacher without the proper Dharma.)

Question: If a bhikṣu does not recite the precepts every half-month, is ignorant of the Dharma (being unaware of the sūtras and vinaya of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna), and is ignorant of various monastic affairs (such as *karmavācanā*, *poṣadha*, and the adjudication of disputes, as well as the two types of fivefold virtues and matters of decorum), yet frequently ordains others (into the homeless life)—acting as the three masters (the *upādhyāya*, the *ācārya*, or the instructor who bestows the precepts)—does he incur any offense?
Answer: Such a person should not even consume the offerings of the faithful, let alone...

On Ordaining Others (If a bhikṣu does not recite the precepts, yet drinks water and eats rice, he commits the offense of theft day after day; therefore it is said that he "should not," etc. Being himself muddled, he cannot cause others to be clear, and thus this rule was established.

Having received full ordination, one should be diligent and energetic as if extinguishing a fire on one's head. One must only learn the precepts in the presence of a wise bhikṣu. Be careful not to be indolent, lazy, or negligent! [Question 5: On Ordaining Disciples by Theft]).

Question: If a person whose parents or the laws of the state do not permit them [to leave home], and whom a bhikṣu takes away by force without asking their master and ordains (one who has taken what was not given), what offense does he commit?
Answer: He commits a grave offense. Because it involves theft, it constitutes a *pārājika* (an offense involving expulsion). [The following examples are not limited to this case alone.

If a government official’s runaway slave flees to a bhikṣu to enter the monastic life, and the bhikṣu, knowing this, allows him to stay, he commits a grave offense even before the formal ordination. [This is because it concerns property belonging to another; since it is so even before ordination, how much more so afterward.]

How much more so for one who steals and ordains others! In the Dharma-ending age, bhikṣus frequently engage in such matters; they are neither meticulous nor careful, they do not examine the person's background, and they act with reckless arrogance and falsehood. Therefore, they ought to commit a grave offense and must certainly be restrained against this. (This concludes the sixth inquiry: "Acting as a Teacher to One’s Father.")
Question: If a son has already left the household life (becoming a bhikṣu) and his parents later leave the household life to seek refuge with their son, may that son ordain them?

(May he permit them to leave the household life, study the Path, and practice the Dharma? Answer: He may [permit them to] leave the household life and study the Path. Taking principle as the primary concern, one discusses only the Buddha-Dharma and does not adhere to worldly etiquette. Since he is already capable of delivering others, all such cases may be delivered.

Thus, for example, King Śuddhodana prostrated before the Tathāgata, and Queen Māyā listened to the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma; therefore, it is said that they may be delivered. Otherwise, if one dwells in the notions of "self" and "mine," one cannot deliver others by violating the precepts. (End of Question Seven).

Question: If there is a bhikṣu who has violated the precepts, is he permitted to ordain others? Answer: If he has committed a grave offense (pārājika), there is no longer any principle by which he may ordain others.

Since he has committed an offense involving expulsion, he can no longer even be called a bhikṣu; because he has lost his precepts, he is like a leaking boat that cannot carry one across. Therefore, it is said that this principle does not exist. [The following begins the opening section: If he has committed an offense that is subject to formal adjudication...

The same applies to those who have not yet completed five years of ordination (as can be understood from the preceding examples). If one commits other minor precepts, such as the *pāyattika* offenses, it is necessary to perform confession.

Only then can one attain deliverance (once purified through repentance, one may finally become a teacher and model for others; even a slight lack of purity is unacceptable, how much more so a grave offense? Therefore, the rule was established: [to] request another to act on one's behalf in asking the eighth question).

Question: If a layperson (*avadātavasana*) approaches a certain bhikṣu desiring to leave the household life, and that bhikṣu accepts him [as a candidate], yet is himself unable to serve as his preceptor (*upādhyāya*), he then requests another to act as the ordination preceptor (*karmakāraka-ācārya*).
Is the bhikṣu who first received the candidate's submission still considered a teacher (*ācārya*), or is he not? Answer: He is not a teacher.

[He is not the upādhyāya, and since he does not fulfill the title of the primary teacher (*mūla-ācārya*), he is excluded from this status]. However, if he later transmits the Dharma to the recipient, he may be considered a Dharma-preacher (*dharma-bhāṇaka*). (Alternatively, there may be no further Dharma remaining to be received.)

As for those who merely follow [a teacher], they may serve as a *niśrayācārya* (reliance teacher), but they can never be called an *upādhyāya* (preceptor), because they have not received the precepts from them. Those who indiscriminately refer to such persons as "teachers" should take heed of this.
(Regarding the ninth point: one who ordains others must instruct them; see the inquiry.)
Question: If a bhikṣu ordains many disciples, acting as two masters (the upādhyāya and the ācārya), yet fails to instruct them in the precepts, what offense does he commit?

Answer: He commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. Why is this? Because he fails to instruct them due to indolence and out of attachment to his own kin. (The following provides scriptural evidence.

Long ago, in the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, there was a bhikṣu who ordained disciples but did not instruct them in the precepts; they committed many unrighteous acts (such as violating the prohibitions). Because they lacked instruction and admonition, they were unable to repent. (The following clarifies the resulting retribution.)
As retribution, at the end of his life he was reborn among the dragons. [The nature of the dragons is such that] they must undergo suffering;

once every seven days, when their time for retribution arrives, fire burns their bodies until the flesh is consumed and only the bones remain. Immediately thereafter, it is restored, and then it is burned again. Unable to endure the suffering, he looked back upon his past causes and reflected to himself:
"By what sin in my former life have I come to such suffering? (Because of this suffering, doubt arose and he reproached himself. The dragon possesses the five supernatural powers. Then...
He observed his past lives and saw for himself that he had previously been a śramaṇa who did not uphold the prohibitions and precepts, nor was his teacher instructing him.

(Knowing that his teacher did not teach him the precepts), he immediately conceived a poisonous thought and felt anger toward his original teacher—this is the same as the offense of rebellion against one's father and mother. He resolved to harm him.

(The word "meeting" [huì] should also be understood as "thinking," for it was through this thought that) later, when his teacher happened to come with five hundred people by boat to cross the sea, the dragon then emerged.
A dragon seized a boat. (From within the boat) the people immediately asked, "Who are you? (The dragon) replied, "I am a dragon.
(The people) asked again, "Since you are a dragon, why have you seized this boat? (The dragon) replied, "I require nothing else. If you set down this bhikṣu, I shall release you and let you go;
otherwise, it shall not be so. (The people) asked again, "How does this bhikṣu concern you? Why do you not seek anyone else? [The dragon] did not seek out any other person at all.
"Why do you seek only this bhikṣu? the dragon asked. "He was originally my teacher," he replied. "As a teacher, he ought to have instructed and admonished me;
yet he did not instruct me, and now I suffer this pain. That is why I seek him. While these people were unable to stop him, he intended to seize the bhikṣu and cast him into the water.
The bhikṣu said, "I shall enter the water myself; there is no need for you to seize me. He then threw himself in.

They lose their lives in the water. (This is the retribution for a teacher who fails to provide instruction. The following summarizes the preceding text. Judging by this, one who guides others must not fail to instruct them. (Once one is a teacher of men, one must not neglect instruction.

If one desires good learning but lacks good teaching, "good" will instead turn into "not-good. This is the fault of failing to instruct. Or, if something that was not good becomes good because of the instruction, this is the merit of transformative teaching. Therefore, the Vinaya states: "All disciples should diligently examine themselves.

Otherwise, it will lead them to fail to cultivate wholesome qualities and to dwell in what is unrighteous, like a horse without a halter; the harm caused will not be slight. Thus the Buddha said: "O Bhikṣus, you all..."

"It would be better to act as a butcher and engage in the work of killing than, after granting ordination and full admission (*upasampadā*) to one who has left the household life, to abandon them and fail to inquire after them, thereby causing my True Dharma to perish prematurely.

For this reason, one must strictly examine those disciples; even those who do not comply with admonitions and instructions must be expelled from the monastery. One must be careful not to tolerate them, for such negligence brings harm to both parties. Alas! In recent times, it is often seen that those who offer warnings are insistent, yet those who listen remain oblivious. Whose fault is this?

This [work] is specifically intended as a warning for those who ordain others without providing instruction, and for those who provide instruction but do so poorly; it is written with profound intent. One should reflect that there is no way to repay the great kindness of the Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One, even by crushing one's body or sacrificing one's life. The "Chapter on Ordaining Others" (Shang du ren shi pin) concludes here. Below follows the "Chapter on Receiving [Instruction]" (Xia shou...).
Chapter on the Matter of Precepts (Śīlavastu-varga). Question: Chapter Seven on the Matter of Receiving the Precepts.

Since one who has been delivered from the world must necessarily be conferred with the precepts, and because failing to provide instruction after such deliverance incurs great transgression, the Chapter on Receiving the Precepts follows immediately after the section on delivering others. Regarding the reception of the precepts: it consists of the ritual for the Three Refuges and the formal announcement (*jñapti*).

The four *karmas* (formal ecclesiastical acts) involve this receiving and that bestowing, handed down in succession from one to another. They cause people to reform their evils and follow what is good, to turn away from heterodoxy and return to the orthodox, to reflect inwardly and gather their thoughts, and to realize their own minds—this is what is meant by [the path] leading directly to the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

As for "matters," these refer to such things as violating the precepts or renouncing the precepts, as illustrated by the nineteen questions and answers [beginning with] Question One: "Violating the Precepts Without Repentance."

Question: If a śrāmaṇera violates the ten precepts—namely, (1) not killing, (2) not stealing, and so on up to (10) not handling silver or money, which constitute the ten precepts—what does "violation" mean? It refers to the sense of transgressing, violating, and damaging [the precepts].
Among them, if one has committed one, two, or three precepts and does not repent, can they receive the full ordination (*mahāśramaṇa-saṃvara*)? Answer:

If they remember [the offenses] but do not repent, they cannot [receive it], because their physical vessel is impure and they cannot obtain the pure precepts. Or, if they do not remember at all, or if they do not know the Dharma, they may receive the precepts as before;

however, because they obtained them through an improper method, the following serves as a warning to the preceptor regarding the ritual for receiving the great precepts: the preceptor should ask the śrāmaṇera, "Have you not committed any offense? The śrāmaṇera replies: If he says—

If one has committed an offense, one should immediately be instructed to perform repentance (only then may it be rectified). If the preceptor does not inquire, the master on the altar (the *ācārya*, instructor, etc. should inquire.

If [the preceptor] does not inquire at all, the teacher commits the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. (Be cautious! Those who act as teachers and models must be strict, meticulous, and prioritize careful examination.

Otherwise, before benefiting others, they will first harm themselves; what benefit would there be? [This concludes the second section: Receiving the Great Repentance and Inquiring about the Small Offenses].)
Question: (If a bhikṣu), having received full ordination, may he repent of the transgressions committed while he was a śrāmaṇera? Answer: He may.

(Since there is no concealment and it is beneficial rather than harmful,) the method of confession is the same as when one was a śrāmaṇera; one may confess either before one's preceptor or before a single bhikṣu.

This need not necessarily follow the method for repentance used by the great bhikṣus; yet, even without such repentance, one fears that the Great Precepts may not remain firm. Furthermore, it cannot be treated in the same general manner as others. Regarding those who first committed an offense without remembering it when receiving the Great Precepts, but later remembered and repented—it is because there is a fear that they might remember later and fail to repent that this case is set apart.
(Question Three: On the Incompleteness of Robes and Alms Bowls)
Question: If a śrāmaṇera is on the ordination platform and wishes to receive the full precepts (mahāśīla), should he wear the kāsāya, remove his shoes, and have his head shaved?
Or may he wear secular clothing instead of the kāsāya, have leather footwear on his feet, or lack a robe and bowl, borrowing them for the occasion? Will he obtain the precepts in such cases?

Answer: Regarding those in secular dress, the preceptor must not confer the precepts unless they have been questioned [regarding their faults]. (This is because one fears that they might be followers of internal or external paths who are feigning the intent to receive the precepts. One should know that if the preceptor asks about their transgressions and they are made to reform them, only then may they receive them. As for all others, they may receive them.

(Nevertheless, if the preceptor commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense [due to contempt for the Dharma], since this transgression is no small matter, it would be of no benefit even if [the candidate] were to receive them;

it is clear that in such a case, they ultimately cannot obtain the precepts. Thus, the *Upasampadā-vidhi* states: "These robes and this bowl must be personally prepared by oneself. Whether borrowed or lacking, they are both termed 'unlawful' (*adharmika*). According to the clear judgment of the Vinaya, the precepts are not obtained. One's entire life will then be spent in vain, consuming the offerings of the faithful.")

They will fall into the three miserable realms and wander in saṃsāra for long kalpas without any liberation. Considering this, would it be permissible to borrow robes to receive the precepts? This concerns the fourth inquiry: whether one who has failed to observe the precepts minutely may not abandon them but must receive them again.

Question: If there is a bhikṣu who, without having relinquished the precepts, becomes a śrāmaṇera or a great practitioner (mahāpuruṣa)—this person [is one who] has never transgressed the precepts—or if one falsely assumes the status of a śrāmaṇera out of a desire for fame or to seek superior status, may they receive the precepts again? Answer: They may not. (The fifth inquiry regarding the previous precepts and madness.)

Question: If one does not receive the precepts again, do the precepts previously received still remain? Answer: They remain. (If it is because those who received them previously [still] remain, then the reason why those receiving now do not obtain them is as follows.

However, speaking specifically of the Great Way practitioner (*mahāyānika*), the character "or" (*huo*) in the text should likely be considered a superfluous insertion; it can be understood by viewing [the subject] as a single person. If viewed as two persons, it is incorrect to say they "remain," because the former has committed a transgression and has not relinquished the precepts.)

Why is this? According to the Vinaya, if a bhikṣu commits a grave offense, he must relinquish his precepts and become a śrāmaṇera; even in that case, it is not permitted for him to receive the full precepts again immediately, let alone one who does not relinquish them at all. Therefore, it is stated in general that he may not receive them.

As for the fact that this is not mentioned in the Sūtras, it may be that the translators’ phrasing was insufficient; this cannot be known for certain. One should examine this for oneself. (End of Question Six: On the Right and Wrong of Later Masters).

Question: If one has previously received the precepts from a later teacher, does that [later] teacher count as one's teacher? Answer: No; because the precepts were not obtained through him, he cannot be called a teacher. This was established as a regulation for those who forget their previous [teacher] after receiving [the precepts] later.
(This concludes the seventh question regarding one person acting as a teacher.)
Question: If many people receive the precepts while inviting only one person to serve as their teacher, can ten or five people receive the precepts simultaneously?

Answer: There is no such principle. According to the Vinaya, for the full ordination (upasampadā), all ten teachers must be complete: first, the Upādhyāya; second, the Ācārya; and furthermore, seven witnesses who must be in accordance with the Dharma are required.

All these must be invited to be pure and so forth. If the number does not reach ten, the precepts are not accomplished. Why is this? As the *Jièyí* (Ritual of Ordination) states: "To perfectly accomplish the three clusters [of training], one must rely upon the three teachers; to raise up and examine the seven non-transgressions, one entirely depends upon the seven witnesses."

Therefore, it is necessary that there be exactly ten people before one may be ordained; this is the rule for the initial assembly. Regarding the "ten in equal numbers," the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* permits only three people to receive ordination together, and even four is not allowed, because [if more than three are present], they would be treating a non-quorum as a quorum while performing the *karmavācanā*.

This contradicts the principle; therefore, it is said in general that such a principle does not exist. It is necessary that one receive the precepts sequentially at different times. However, if the assembly of monks is too large and one cannot wait for the sequence, or if it is appropriate to temporarily employ a skillful means, it is permissible for many people to receive them simultaneously.
Otherwise, one should follow the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, which takes one or two persons as the standard [for receiving precepts from two masters]. (Question 8 on Receiving Precepts from Two Masters).
Question: If a śrāmaṇera receives the full precepts (the complete set of rules, etc.), he requests one bhikṣu to serve as his preceptor for the full ordination.
However, this bhikṣu does not know the ritual procedures (*karmavācanā*) or the method for conferring the precepts. He then requests another person on his behalf to confer the precepts upon him.
Between these two—the former and the latter—who should be considered the preceptor? Answer: The one who actually confers the precepts upon him is the preceptor; the former bhikṣu is not.

One who bestows the dharma of the precepts is not necessarily a teacher (the *karmavācanā* method consists of one motion and three proclamations, as well as matters such as exhortation and interrogation; however, one who wishes to serve as a model for others should have a profound understanding of the three contemplations).

To master the two forms of upholding, the five virtues, and the ten recitations, and to achieve both teaching and practice—this is permissible. Otherwise, if one’s own affairs are not clear while wishing to act as a teacher for others, it is improper. (The Ninth Question: When a Teacher Does Not Accord with the Dharma)

Question: (At the time of receiving the precepts,) if the masters and witnesses on the platform—the three masters and seven witnesses—wear secular clothing instead of the *kāṣāya*, or have violated the prohibitions and lost their status as *bhikṣus*, does the recipient obtain the precepts?
Answer: If the person receiving the precepts (as a disciple) knows that [the masters wearing] secular clothing and so forth is contrary to the Dharma, they do not obtain them.

(This is because, by giving rise to doubt or mental agitation, there is one who is impure; according to the Sūtras, if even one person is impure, your precept-observance will certainly not be accomplished. If they do not know [this], they obtain them. (Because they do not know whether it is right or wrong.)

Although the master may have faults, if the disciple is sincere and their faith is so earnest that they are free from all doubt, they will attain [the precepts]. This is precisely what is meant by the saying: "Faith is the source of the Way and the mother of merit. Since the transmission from master to master has no bearing on the disciple, [it is said]:
"If one does not know how to receive the precepts" (Question Ten).
Question: At the time of receiving the precepts, if the assembly of monks is not in harmony, or if they strike or revile one another, does the recipient obtain the precepts?

(Is it certain? Answer: If the monks on the platform are in harmony, then [the recipient] obtains them. If the monks on the platform are not in harmony, [the recipient] does not obtain them. (The preciousness of the Saṃgha lies in the six kinds of harmony: harmony of body in dwelling together; harmony of speech in being without contention;

harmony of mind in mutual joy; harmony of precepts in practicing together; harmony of views in sharing the same understanding; and harmony of benefits in equal distribution. Only those who are thus may be called the Saṃgha. Since they are currently striking and reviling one another and are not in harmony, they do not belong to the class of the Saṃgha.)

However, if the assembly is not in harmony, it does not concern the recipient of the precepts; it is sufficient that the presiding master (*karmācārya*) be in harmony. If this [assembly] is not in harmony, one may wait for it to become harmonious before receiving the precepts—this is also permissible (Question Eleven on Receiving the Precepts at the Time of Taking Them).

Question: If one wishes to receive the precepts, is there a specific time or season for it? Answer: Only the final watch of the night (the last part of the night) is not permitted, because the date and time would be difficult to determine.

During the first or middle watches of the night, if lamps are available, it is acceptable; however, if there are no lamps or candles, it is also not permitted, because the parties would be unable to see one another. It is essential that they behold each other’s physical forms before the precepts can be received.

The transmission of the precepts must proceed from teacher to teacher in succession. One must behold the teacher’s form as if beholding the countenance of a saint; only when one can give rise to faith and joy, and develop a heart of gladness, may the precepts be received. Without a lamp, one cannot perceive [the teacher].
Thus, it is not permitted. However, it should be understood that the midday is the correct time. (End of Question 12: Moving the Altar to Receive the Precepts). Question:
If, at the time of receiving the precepts, it happens to rain, and one moves the site of the ceremony under a roof to receive the precepts, does one obtain the precepts?

(Question: Is the *śīmaṇḍala* [ordination site] not a building? It is also exposed ground, because one seeks to exit the three realms. Answer: If one wishes to relocate the *śīmaṇḍala*, it is also permissible to receive the precepts under a roof;

however, one must first dissolve the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*). Once [the boundary] under the roof has been re-established as a *śīmaṇḍala*, having a place of reliance and support, one may then receive the precepts.
Otherwise, it is not permitted, because there is no *śīmaṇḍala* to rely upon. (End of the thirteenth inquiry regarding whether the precepts are obtained.)
Question: If, at the time of receiving the precepts, there should be some obstacle such that one does not reach completion, is this person a *mahābhikṣu*?

Answer: Once the three *karmavācanās* have been concluded, he is indeed a *mahābhikṣu*. It should be understood that if the three *karmas* have not yet been entrusted [to the assembly], one has not yet obtained the precepts. The obstacles are as described above, such as water, fire, and so forth. "Completion" refers to the period after the three *karmavācanās*.

Furthermore, the four [teachings] that follow the four reliances (*pratisaraṇa*)—the teachings on the disclosure of reality and so forth—are no different [from what has been explained before]. Therefore, the detailed explanation in the subsequent text is the same as previously discussed (see Question 14).

Question: When a *śrāmaṇera* receives the *bhikṣu* precepts, he completes the thirteen matters [of the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*]. If the various precept masters and the *upādhyāya* do not subsequently continue to instruct him in the precepts, does he obtain the full set of precepts? Answer:
If the masters do not provide instruction, yet when the *poṣadha* is recited on the fifteenth day, he listens with a focused mind, he then obtains the complete set.

(This follows the precedent that once the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* is concluded, one immediately obtains the full precepts. Regarding "completing the ten," etc.: on the platform, the precept master merely indicates the two categories of heavy offenses—the four *pārājika* and the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

Regarding the latter three sections and so forth, as for those who do not continue the teaching, it may be because they have specific circumstances or conditions. As for "concentrating the mind" and so forth, this is because at the time of reciting the precepts (*śīla*), one must necessarily explain the characteristics of the precepts in full. The Sarvāstivādins say: "One obtains the full precepts (*upasaṃpad*) upon the completion of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal motion followed by three proclamations).

The subsequent explanation of the four *anuvartana*, the four *niśraya*, the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, and so forth, is merely for the sake of knowledge. Therefore, without receiving the three refuges (*tri-śaraṇa*), one does not obtain the five precepts; without the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, one does not obtain the full precepts. Once the three refuges have been received, one has already obtained the five [precepts].

Regarding the Precepts: The reason for stating the names of the five precepts at the end is to enable the person before one to recognize the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the precepts. Furthermore, it is said that after the three refuges are completed, by stating the single precept of non-killing, the five precepts are fully established;

this is because if one can maintain even one, one can maintain all five, and because the spheres of influence of the five precepts are mutually integrated. Moreover, it is because the original intention was to vow to receive the five precepts. (Question Fifteen: On the Insufficiency of Robes).

Question: If one wishes to receive the precepts but does not possess the three robes (*tricīvara*), yet possesses the value for them—whether they have been dyed or undyed, or cut or uncut—is it permissible to use these as the actual robes?

Answer: In all cases, it is not permissible. [These are] merely names without reality, for they cause one to lose dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*). This will be clarified in the following section on the Three Robes. One must receive the precepts with the three robes fully complete; not even one is lacking.

Even if one has the price for the robes and so forth, since the actual robes themselves are not yet obtained, it is in every case impermissible. As explained above regarding borrowing and the like, not only is the precept not obtained, but in the future one will instead fall into the three miserable realms (*trāya-patha*). What benefit is there in that?

Those who merely wish to receive the precepts must by no means act with haste; for before they have attained its merit, they will first invite its faults. Is this not to be treated with caution? (The sixteenth point on why the assembly cannot be uniform).

Question: At the time of receiving the precepts, if it is difficult to assemble a fixed number of the Sangha due to various circumstances, how many monks are required to confer the full ordination (mahānāśī)?

[Question] Answer: With the exception of the three masters, one may [perform the ordination] with five or more monks from outside [the immediate circle]. (If this were considered entirely valid, it would be the same as the previous explanations regarding the three masters and seven witnesses;

having six is also permissible. However, this is merely a temporary expedient and not the permanent Dharma. Some say that the "seven witnesses" symbolizes the breaking of the seven heinous acts. During the Buddha’s lifetime there were seven such cases, but now there is no instance of shedding the Buddha’s blood; therefore, it is said that five or six are also acceptable. [End of section on] Deceitful Arrogance, Question Seventeen.

Question: If a *śrāmaṇera* has previously falsely claimed to be a "Great Way-man" (*mahāpuruṣa*) and received the prostrations of a *mahābhikṣu*, may he later receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*)?

Answer: He may not. (The term "prostration," *li*, refers to the act of treading; it involves measured progress and retreat, and a distinct hierarchy of honor. It is called "prostration" because one uses the most honored head to pay homage to the lowest part of the feet, representing the ultimate degree of reverence.

Since that person lacks both honor and status, his false claim was improper; by claiming what he had not attained, he commits the grave offense of lying. Such a person is called a "thief who steals the *kaṭhina* robe" or one who "dwells as a thief. The Buddha did not permit such a person to be ordained; therefore, it is said that he may not [receive ordination]. This concludes the first inquiry regarding dependence (*niśraya*) in that place.
18). Question:

If a śrāmaṇera takes leave of his teacher to travel elsewhere, and due to some difficult circumstance or obstacle he is unable to return, should he immediately request a teacher for dependence (*niśraya*) at that location and receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*)?
Is the precept obtained? Answer: The precept is obtained (the difficulty of the circumstances does not hinder it). If the teacher is qualified according to the Dharma, one should receive it.
Because neither party is at fault, they obtain [the precepts] (The nineteenth question on the seduction of śrāmaṇeras).

Question: If a bhikṣu who likes to act as a teacher seduces another śrāmaṇera, takes him to a different community (*saṃgha*), and confers the full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon him, what offense does he commit?
Should that other community listen to and accept [the candidate], knowing that he was seduced by another bhikṣu? Answer: If his [original] teacher has committed a transgression...

Regarding religious matters (such as committing a root offense against the major precepts, or even engaging in improper acts such as selling goods): the śrāmaṇera and those who accompany him are without fault. (The character "jié" [及] means "to pursue" or "to follow along.")

If one follows along with the opportunity, it will be beneficial and cause no harm; the bhikṣu incurs no offense. However, if the teacher has committed an unrighteous act and yet leads [the disciple] away, the bhikṣu commits a grave offense (saṃghāvaśeṣa), and the śrāmaṇera incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma (vinayātikrama).

If the teacher on the ordination platform belongs to a different community and the monks already know [of his misconduct], they should not confer the precepts upon him. If, without investigating the circumstances of his arrival, they nevertheless confer the precepts, they commit an offense of forfeiture and transgression (naiḥsargika-pāyattika), because this violates the Buddha’s word.
To cite proof from the past: once there was an elder bhikṣu who had only a single śrāmaṇera to attend to him, and no others.
A certain bhikṣu would repeatedly entice a śrāmaṇera away. This elderly bhikṣu was left without anyone to look after him, and before long he passed away.
Because of this, the precept was established: one must not entice another's śrāmaṇera away. To entice another's śrāmaṇera away constitutes a grave offense.

(The former was established because of old age; the latter was established because of illness. If there is a bhikṣu who sees another śrāmaṇera attending to an elderly or sick person, [the bhikṣu] should instruct...

He should cause him to leave. If the śrāmaṇera departs, this bhikṣu commits a grave offense. (This is because the bhikṣu, out of greed, harms others for his own sake and destroys his own good intention.
The Chapter on Receiving Precepts above is concluded; next is the Chapter on Receiving Offerings.)

Chapter Eight: On Receiving Alms (Following the Chapter on Receiving Precepts; concerning those who receive alms. A bhikṣu who has received the precepts is worthy to be a field of merit for humanity. There may be donors who offer the four requisites and other items;

whether a bhikṣu should accept them or not, as there are various differing circumstances, these matters should also be clarified through questions. Thus, there are twenty-seven question-and-answer sections [The First: Questions on Attaining Merit through Receiving Alms]).

Question: If a bhikṣu accepts an invitation from a donor for the fourfold offerings (the four requisites: food and drink, clothing, bedding, and medicine), may he share the items received with others? Answer: He may.

(To diminish one’s own benefit for the sake of others, or to give to those suffering from hunger and thirst, brings inexhaustible merit. This is the primary purpose of the distribution of goods: it manifests his lack of greed. It is logically appropriate to act thus; therefore, it is said that he "may.
[This concludes the second question regarding requests exceeding the standard allotment].

Question: (Regarding the sequence of a bhikṣu’s rainy-season retreat,) having accepted an invitation for the four requisites for an extended period, he may go out on account of some minor matter (such as matters concerning his parents).
May one eat food from outside [the monastery] and take medicine from outside? (Taking it means to subdue [the afflictions], or to use decoctions and medicines to harmonize the four great elements.

Answer: One may take them if the donor permits (because they universally desire to cause people to cultivate merit; if not permitted, one may not take them, as it would contravene the donor’s wishes and give rise to censure). As the ancients said: "The Teacher has issued a command, exhorting the bhikṣus: 'Advancing on the Path and adorning the person, the three things are always insufficient;
do not greedily seek beyond what is allotted, but should rather reflect within yourselves. (This concludes the third inquiry regarding receiving through deception out of greed.)

Question: (If) another person wishes to give an object to a bhikṣu, they should first ask whether the bhikṣu has it or not. (Confucius showed kindness to those in distress; the administration of Qi gave priority to the widowed.)
Therefore, when asked whether [an item] exists or not, if a bhikṣu actually possesses it himself, he should not falsely claim it does not exist out of greed to deceive the donor.

If the other person then gives the object to that bhikṣu, what offense has this bhikṣu committed? Answer: By taking it with a greedy mind, he commits the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (the forfeiture offense);

by lying—claiming it does not exist when it does—he commits a *pāyattika* (offense requiring confession). Thus, there are two layers of offenses: first, greed; second, falsehood. The suffering resulting from such a fall is profound and not slight; one must certainly guard against it. [The Elder asks the assembly specifically on the fourth case.]
Question: If the Sangha’s food is given exclusively to the *upādhyāya* (senior monk), may the *upādhyāya* eat it? (*Upādhyāya* refers to one who has held the full precepts for thirty or forty years;

those with twenty or ten years of seniority are termed *madhyama* or *navaka*. Those with fewer than these are merely to be respected; they possess the title of *upādhyāya* but have not yet reached the actual rank. Answer: If the *upādhyāya* eats it with a greedy mind, he commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

(In the world-transcending Great Matter, the elimination of greed, hatred, and delusion is considered the most urgent. Since he is called an *upādhyāya*, he should know this for himself. Although he may labor diligently for the sake of the community, it is only reasonable that he receive a portion of the offerings.)

There is no fault in being without greed; it is greed that incurs transgression. As in the *Saṃgharakṣita-sūtra*, an elder, driven by a greedy mind, fell even into hell and underwent the sufferings of taking birth as a camel and being burned by fire while crying out in agony. How can one not be cautious! (The fifth question: seeking fine food through deception).
Question: (If) a bhikṣu who is not ill falsely claims to have the suffering of illness—(or speaks falsely of the suffering of wind, heat, and so forth)—in order to seek out choice food.

(Regarding the craving for milk, curd, and similar items: Having obtained them, what offense does one commit? Answer: One commits a grave offense. (This is false and greedy covetousness, no different from theft; because it deceives those worthy of compassion, it constitutes a grave sin.
[Question Six: On Receiving Food while Violating Proper Decorum])

Question: (If a bhikṣu) receives food without wearing the three robes, what offense does he commit? Answer: He commits an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). [Note: It is permitted to wear the great robe (*saṃghāṭī*) when begging for alms.]

The seven robes are worn when attending a formal meal; the five robes are worn for ordinary meals. Furthermore, it is not merely a matter of eating; one who maintains the robes must never be separated from the third robe (the *kāṣāya*) at any time. Only then is one called a true practitioner of the Vinaya. To disregard the Buddha’s words and seek only convenience is improper.
Therefore, one incurs this offense. (Regarding the "Requesting Persons," it is necessary to chant the question;

this is the seventh point). Question: When a *dānapati* has just requested two or three persons, must the assembly chant [the names]? Answer: It is necessary to chant them. (Those who chant should be appointed by the administrative officers (*karmadāna*) in successive order of rotation;

one must not bypass the sequence. All visiting monks have a share in the offerings (*lābha*), and without chanting, these would not be clear. Therefore, it is necessary to chant them. (Regarding "Monks and Nuns," both may ask; this is the eighth point).

Question: When the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) for distributing items among the great *bhikṣu* saṃgha is being performed, if a *bhikṣuṇī* enters within the boundary (*sīmā*), should she receive a share?

Answer: She should receive it. These items being distributed are the property of the present Saṃgha of the ten directions; since a *bhikṣuṇī* is also counted as part of the Saṃgha, she should receive a share. Otherwise, by making a distinction between "self" and "other," one will incur the retribution of stinginess. One who maintains the Dharma must not fail to know this. (The ninth question concerning the equal distribution of shares before and after.)
Question: Suppose a person, whether a monastic or a layperson, entrusts an object as an offering to the *saṃgha* present at a specific location.

When the object arrives later and other bhikṣus come and are seated for the distribution, should they receive a share? Answer: If the *ghanṭā* (wooden gong) is struck—because this is done to include the *saṃgha* of the ten directions—they should receive a share.

Not to distribute it would be a transgression. If the *ghanṭā* is not struck, they do not receive it. Why? Because this object was originally offered to a single location; since it is not for the sake of the ten directions, it is reasonable that it should not be distributed. Therefore, it is said they do not receive it. (From the *Daòxíng shòushī wèn*).
(10). Question: If a bhikṣu is on the road and a woman offers him an object, may he accept it? Answer: If she is a relative or someone he knows, he may take it without fault.

If she is not someone he knows and he accepts it, he will incur the reproach of others; he must not accept it, for to do so constitutes an offense. The Vinaya stipulates that one must not beg for objects from a woman who is not a relative. (From the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-saṃghabhedaka-vastu*).
(Section Eleven: The Question on Receiving Gifts from Nuns). Question:
If a bhikṣu is traveling on a road and a bhikṣuṇī offers him an object, may he accept it? Answer: If it is offered to the Saṃgha, he may accept it.

"Saṃgha" refers to the assembly. Receiving [the precepts] in accordance with the assembly involves no fault. One must not receive them if there is no assembly (as in receiving them alone when no assembly is present), for one fears public censure; therefore it is said "it is not permitted. (The same as the Vinaya regulations, etc.
[End of the twelfth question on the previous boundary]).
Question: If rice for a monastic meal has been offered by a donor to a specific group of monks, and that group has already departed, may the host of the meal offer it to monks who arrive later?

Will those later arrivals be permitted to eat? Answer: If the later-arriving monks strike the *ghanṭā* (wooden gong), they may eat. This is because they possess the intention to serve the community and do not take [the food] for private gain.

If they do not strike the *ghanṭā*, eating it constitutes a *pārājika* offense. [The gong] reaches all ten directions; whether one is before or after [the original group], one should rightfully receive the food. If the *ghanṭā* is not struck, this meal originally belongs to the ten directions, and thus the later arrivals [are entitled to it].
To eat alone is to steal the property of the Sangha of the ten directions; therefore, one commits a *pārājika* offense (from the thirteenth question of the *Paścādvibhāga-pūrvadṛṣṭi*).

Question: If on the eighth day of the fourth month there is an offering (*dakṣiṇā*)—this being the offering for the Great Assembly on the occasion of the Buddha’s birth—and on the fifteenth day of the seventh month the resident monks have already departed...

(The monk who received the offerings at the Great Assembly) is the one from whom the Abbot takes [the portion] for the monks who arrive after the assembly. If the monks who arrive later divide and take [a share], what offense do they commit?

Answer: If the *gandi* was struck, the present monks may divide it together without fault. If the *gandi* was not struck, the later monks may not take a share; those who divide it commit the offense of theft.

Since the offerings of the Great Assembly belong to the monks of the ten directions, to privately appropriate them for the ten directions when the *gandi* was not struck constitutes an offense of *pārājika*, as before. Alternatively, if the value does not reach five *kārsāpaṇas*, one should calculate the gravity of the offense accordingly.
[It is] to be known: [Section on] Receiving Previous Alms-Donations (Question 14).

Question: If a layperson has prepared items for alms-donation (*dakṣiṇā*)—“prepared” here meaning “already offered”—and rather than lending them out, [the donor] intends to give them first to the original recipient (*pūrvapudgala*), but that original recipient has already departed, and they subsequently offer them to another person;
may this other person accept them? Answer: They should accept them. However, one must still ask the owner.

(One should immediately ask this layperson, or the person in charge, etc. "Will the original owner definitely return? If the host replies, "He will never return," then one may take it by means of a blessing-rite (*paritta*) without fault.

If he says, "He might return," then one must not take it; if one takes it, one commits the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. Because [the answer] was either "he might return" or "he will not return," one commits only the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

If one knows for certain that he will return and yet deliberately takes it, one commits the offense of *pārājika*. Why is it an offense of *pārājika*? It is because it is the property of the Sangha from the four directions; therefore, one commits *pārājika*. It is certain.

This careful examination is undertaken solely out of fear that the relationship between cause and effect may be unclear, thereby obstructing the Path and preventing the accomplishment of supramundane karma. (Question Fifteen: On Transforming Livelihood for the Sake of Giving).
Question: If a *bhikṣu* who earns a living acquires goods and gives them as clothing or food to another *bhikṣu*, may that other *bhikṣu* accept them?
Answer: If he takes the clothing, he commits an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*), because he has accepted impure objects with a mind of greed and pride.

However, if he is in dire straits and there is no place to obtain food, that [earning *bhikṣu*] may have a layperson prepare food [with the acquired goods], and the other *bhikṣu* may eat it. Nevertheless, [the earning] practitioner...
If one announces to the assembly, saying, "This object is not my own; it belongs to such-and-such a person," then it may be eaten.

If the master of the trade does not announce it to the assembly, and the bhikṣu eats it, he commits a *pāyattika* offense. [Question: What if there is no assembly? [Answer: Two or three people may also be announced as the assembly (for two or three may also be designated as a "gathering").
If the practitioner of the Way gives the object as a gift to another person, and that other person says, "This is my property; you may eat it," [the object belongs to that person].

Others [claim] it is not because it is impure; yet, that one must perform such various circuitous actions to practice the Dharma indicates that such a person certainly lacks the principle of "earning a livelihood" (*jīvikā*). As for earning a livelihood, whether through providing for one's needs or through trade and commerce, the pursuit of profit is an extremely grave fault.

This is why it is said one would rather be a butcher than a merchant, as detailed in the Vinaya. These are things by which one’s life is sustained through impurity; even a pure bhikṣu incurs offense by consuming them, let alone one who earns a living through such means.

The purpose is to cause this person to feel shame within themselves, so that they dare not again engage in such impure matters. A bhikṣu must maintain right livelihood (*samyagājīva*) through means such as begging for alms; therefore, this is specifically established as a precept. (End of the sixteenth inquiry: "Can one obtain goods by selling items?")
Question: May a bhikṣu take out [a portion] of the goods? Answer: He may not. (If he does,) he commits an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).

Since this occurs within the section on receiving offerings, in my humble opinion, this word "take out" (*chu*) certainly does not mean "to take out a share" (*chūn-fen*). If it were taken as "taking out," it would mean "releasing it. Even so, the intent of the text is merely that the recipient's intention is lost; it appears as if the object has flowed out from another person's bag, never having been intended for giving to someone.

If a bhikṣu takes it, because he harbors a mind of greed and pride, he commits an offense of expiation involving forfeiture. For instance, if one were to take out a share and depart, what would one cause another to forfeit? Therefore, the question above asks "may he take it? and the answer below says "he may not. Let the wise examine this in detail. [Next: Question regarding excessive greed in accepting invitations. Number [X].
17). Question:

(A bhikṣu) has accepted a donor’s invitation for a period of one hundred days. During this interval, may he accept one meal or two meals from another person? (Regarding the practice of taking one or two meals.

Answer: He may do so if the donor permits it; he may not if the donor does not permit it. (The donor does not permit it because they fear that by accepting further invitations elsewhere, the bhikṣu will reduce the merit accruing to themselves.)
Because this violates the superior intention of the previous donor, one does not [gain merit]. (Question 18: On the Light Disparagement of Donated Objects).
Question: If a bhikṣu, while eating, either spits out a mouthful after having taken it in, or takes a morsel of rice and discards it;

Question: Is this an offense? Answer: It is an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (舍墮). This is because one failed to observe the five contemplations regarding food. If there is any remaining food, one should either empower it with mantras and, with a sincere heart, offer it to a pure place so that ghosts and spirits may partake, or have birds and such eat it;

in these cases, there is merit and no fault. If one spits it out or discards it, this constitutes treating the *dāna* (檀那) of the faithful as something base. A single drop of the faithful’s offering is difficult to digest [and thus misused]; therefore, one incurs this offense. (The nineteenth question: On eating long after the meal and giving it to others.)
Question: (If a bhikṣu) begs for alms, may he give away any surplus he obtains? Answer: If he had no intention of greed at the time of begging, he may take what is in excess.

When one receives alms for sentient beings, if there is a surplus from begging, it should be divided into four parts: one part to give to a fellow practitioner, one part to a destitute beggar, one part to be given as alms to hungry ghosts and animals, and one part for oneself to eat; yet, one must remain free from a mind of greed.

"It is permissible if there is a surplus occasionally. However, it is not permissible if one takes more out of a greedy mind. If there are no sentient beings [to eat them], place them on the top of a tree.
If there are sentient beings who eat the good ones, and if there are none [left], you may take them yourself the next day after washing them with water.

You must not discard them, for the gift of faith is weighty. (To discard them is a transgression; a bhikṣu may not receive what has not been offered. How could he take it himself? The reason he may take it himself again is that...

Because there is no owner. This is like the method of taking food in Uttarakuru (the Northern Continent). There, food and clothing grow spontaneously wherever one is; people simply take them as needed, for there is no one who holds ownership over them.

However, in the Vinaya, the prohibition against receiving food kept overnight is due to a concern for preserving life and a fear of illness. In this case, taking [food] again [after it has been set aside] is because of a concern for the faithful offerings (*śraddhā-deya*); it is adapted to circumstances through skillful means and is not fixed. This should be understood. (This concludes the twentieth section: On Receiving Food Kept Overnight).

Question: If a host is earnest and desires to provide constant offerings to the bhikṣus, may they accept such a long-term invitation? Answer: There are three circumstances under which it may be accepted; otherwise, it is not appropriate.

What are the three? If the host’s location is a place where one can practice the Path, and if there are neither obstacles nor deficiencies [in provisions]—these being the three benefits—one may go to accept their long-term invitation;

otherwise, one should not. Even if one obtains food there, because there is no benefit for attaining the Path, one must not go. (The host’s representative asks on behalf of the host; this is the twenty-first.)

Question: If a host invites [a bhikṣu] for a meal, and the bhikṣu has some other business, may he send another person in his stead? Answer: If the host’s intention is not fixed [on that specific person], it is permissible.

However, if the host objects to the substitution, one commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. (This is because, having specifically invited this person and not that one, one instead causes them to be disparaged and discouraged;
hence this offense. [End of] Question Twenty-two: On Bhikṣus and Ghostly Food.)

Question: If one encounters food belonging to Hārītī (the Mother of Demons), may a bhikṣu eat it? Answer: One may eat it after performing the ritual of incantation and aspiration (*pranidhāna*). This applies not only to this case;

whenever there is food belonging to deities associated with incense and lamps, one must likewise perform the incantation and aspiration before eating. As for the incantation, one may do as one pleases. As for the aspiration, one should pray that the spirits such as Hārītī may quickly transcend to the Pure Land, and that the donor who gives the food may increase in merit and wisdom.

If one happens to encounter such food unexpectedly and there is no other place to obtain food, then it is permissible. Otherwise, it is not. (This concludes the twenty-third direct inquiry on giving raw food to living beings.)
Question: (If) a host wishes to provide for a bhikṣu, but lacks sufficient wealth, and instead offers a cow, a horse, a slave, or the value of food, may the bhikṣu accept them?

Answer: He may accept and use them (out of compassion for the objects; however, they may only be used within his own household). He must not sell them (for selling would cause harm; therefore it is not permitted).

If offered bows, swords, or any other weapons, none of these may be accepted (as these are instruments that injure and destroy living beings; to accept them would be detrimental and of no benefit, and furthermore, they are taboo; therefore, they must not be accepted).
Be careful of this. (The twenty-fourth question following the conclusion of the *zhāi* [fasting retreat]). Question:

Suppose a person provides their own goods to offer to the assembly of monks for the *zhāi*. When the *zhāi* is concluded, these monks have already departed, leaving behind the remaining goods. Later, other monks arrive.

"May one eat? He replied: "If the *gandī* is struck, one may eat without fault; if it is not struck, one commits the offense of theft. (This is as explained above regarding the twelve-fold rice offering for the fast-day [uposatha].
Question Twenty-Five: Receiving Food from a Shared Tray.)

Question: If two bhikṣus eat from a single dish, each having half, and after they have finished eating, one takes the other’s portion; what offense is committed? Answer: If he asks [the owner] and the owner consents to his eating it, there is no offense.

If he does not ask, or if he intentionally takes the food without consent, he commits a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation), because he has touched another’s property improperly and caused them mental agitation.

If he eats without asking at all, he likewise commits a *pāyattika*. Why is there no offense when he asks and receives consent? It is because they have both raised their hands together [in a gesture of shared acceptance].

(One must certainly yield to one another. If the other person extends their hand upward to give, it is no fault to receive with one's own hand extended upward. "Upward" signifies an attitude of reverence. This rule was established for those who are greedy for food. [Question 26: On Taking Pleasure in Committing Offenses].)
Question: If a bhikṣu asks for an object from someone, and that person asks whether it is a "good" bhikṣu (meaning: "I shall give to one who is good;

I will not give to one who is not good"), and the requesting bhikṣu says, "He is a good bhikṣu," and receives the object, what offense does he commit? Answer: If it is actually good and he says it is good, he commits a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation).

(If one who is actually virtuous speaks of possessing precepts and other qualities out of a greedy mind to praise oneself, one incurs this offense. To speak of what is not good as being good (is equivalent to the offense of a great lie). This constitutes a *pārājika* offense (for violating the precepts for the sake of material gain).
One loses the conduct of a bhikṣu; therefore, one incurs this offense. Be cautious! (The twenty-seventh question on returning objects given). Question:
If a bhikṣu gives away all his surplus belongings to another person (merely to relieve their temporary lack), but after giving them says, "I wish to use these later;
you must return them to me," and then takes them back from that person—is this permissible? Answer: It is permissible (though it is better to give them to someone trustworthy).
Regarding "one who is trustworthy": because there has been a breach of agreement, one should subsequently speak to another person, saying, "I have given my property to such-and-such a bhikṣu.

[If that person] takes it back and speaks of it, one must not take it immediately. If a bhikṣu speaks untruthfully and takes it, he incurs an offense; this also constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (an offense requiring forfeiture). This concludes the Chapter on Receiving Gifts.
