[The Buddha said: "If there is another bhikṣu who has been entrusted with authority, and [a third person] begs from that [authorized bhikṣu] and obtains goods, what offense does the one who held the authority commit?

Answer: If one observes that the owner's intention is malicious, one must not [take it]; to take it by force constitutes the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. If one knows the owner's intention is favorable, one may take it.

(In the case of others as well, both the Sangha and the individual are involved in a good deed; neither the giver nor the receiver commits an offense. [This concludes the sixth inquiry concerning bird nests and mouse holes.]
Question: If a dove or a sparrow builds a nest inside a person’s house (or within a monk’s quarters), and a bhikṣu breaks it or blocks the rat holes, what offense does he commit?
Answer: If the dove or sparrow has no young, one may remove the nest; there is no fault in an empty nest. If there are young, one must not do so, for it would cause harm.

As for a rat hole with only a single opening, one must not block it, as this too causes injury and mutilation. It is like the case of Rāhula, who remained in his mother’s womb for six years before being born; had [the opening] been blocked prior to his birth, [he would have perished].

The rat hole [remained closed] for six days. Because the retribution of such a response was thus, if there were internal or external holes, [the rat] would have feared being entangled [in them]. If one manages to block the internal [holes], there will likewise be no obstruction.
Otherwise, it is the opposite: one provides it with food, which is even more marvelous. (This concludes the seventeenth inquiry on the mutual communication of fish and geese.)

Question: May a bhikṣu write letters to his preceptor or his fellow students? (Or rather: if the preceptor-monk and fellow students are separated by distant lands and cannot attend to their duties at the same time, may correspondence be exchanged?

Answer: It is permissible if they are in different regions and their feelings are in accord. (Feeling here refers to propriety. Since they remain within the sphere of human relations, how could they sever ties? Briefly exchanging letters to express greetings and inquiries does not constitute an offense.

However, it is not permitted if they are in different countries. Why? Because travel between different countries is prohibited by royal law. [If one violates this prohibition, one incurs an offense. Question 18.)

Question: If a person leaves the household life against the laws of the state (such as being a soldier, artisan, or cook, or being prohibited by law)—or against the will of their parents (such as being an eldest son or an only son whom the parents love and do not wish to let go)—and thus departs from home in violation of these two constraints, does he obtain the precepts?

Answer: He does not obtain them. According to the Vinaya, even a minor obstruction (*āvaraṇa*) prevents the attainment of the precepts; how much more so when there is a strict command of the state’s law and the compassionate instruction of one's parents?

If one disregards these, one violates the Buddha’s teaching and therefore does not obtain the precepts. To be filial and obedient is itself the precept. Why? Because filial piety is called the precept. Those who today wish to seek ordination should contemplate the Buddha’s teaching and exercise self-restraint accordingly.
The main body of the text is hereby concluded. Below follows the section on the dissemination (the forty-first part: Praise and Request for Dissemination).
At that time—when the questions and answers had finished—Maudgalyāyana rose from his seat and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, you have excellently expounded the Vinaya."

(The Tathāgata has elucidated the Dharma as asked above; it is truly a cause for great joy. However,) after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, during the final five hundred years when Māra is powerful and the Dharma is weak, who will be able to receive and uphold such Vinaya?
(Section Two: Demonstrating and Disseminating. This is further divided into two parts. First: Those with Faith Enter the Path.)

The Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana: "Regarding those who contemplate and study the Vinaya—beings of the final age who possess deep and profound roots of goodness, who, upon hearing such a Dharma as this, contemplate it with joy, and give rise to shame and faith—it should be known that such persons are able to practice this Vinaya.
(2. Those who Slander [the Teaching] and their Saṃsāra)"

The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana: "After my parinirvāṇa, if there are bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs who slander such a Vinaya (as well as the aforementioned study and learning), you should know that these people are companions of Māra and are not my disciples (just as they would have been [if they had lived] in the time of the Buddha).

Such people as these are all heterodox outsiders who hold false views and repudiate emptiness; life after life they will fail to achieve the Way, remaining forever submerged in the sea of suffering and never escaping the three realms."

(III. Summary and Circulation) I now preach this sutra out of compassion for all sentient beings in order to instruct and transform them. If there are those who, as described above, contemplate, study, and practice its teachings, they are true children of the Buddha;
they shall certainly emerge from the ocean of suffering and achieve the Buddha-way. (IV. Faithful Acceptance and Circulation)

At that time, Maudgalyāyana, having heard what the Buddha had taught (concerning matters such as the gravity [of offenses] and so forth), rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (The term "rejoiced" refers to the state of believing and accepting with one's mind; it signifies having attained comprehension and realization.)

To have firm faith without doubt is what is meant by "joyful. To "revere" means to follow and honor; to "practice" means to practice with steadfastness. By means of this very Dharma, one practices for oneself and benefits others, circulating it throughout the heavens and the human world, pervading even the lands within a single mote of dust.

It shall continue through the ten thousand ages of distant realms and sustain the life of wisdom for a thousand autumns, making it eternal and inexhaustible; hence, it is called "faithfully receiving and circulating. Someone may say: "All dharmas from the beginning are eternally in the state of quiescent extinction. Furthermore, a sutra says:

"By practicing the correct contemplation of formlessness, one immediately attains Bodhi. How can one cultivate by means of these five hundred marks and signs? Is this not far too cumbersome? However, they do not realize that the World-Honored One’s teaching has both provisional and ultimate aspects. First, he used the formal characteristics of the *vinaya* precepts to open the way for beginners.

The capacity [of the mind] is subsequently subsumed and returned to the state of no-more-learning by means of the Supreme Vehicle. Thus, the one mind does not obstruct the infinite, and the infinite is not external to the one mind. If the beginner does not maintain the rules of discipline, their unrestrained laxity will result entirely in false views.

If the subsequent mind does not reach the true reality (*dharmatā*), and one’s diligent cultivation remains ultimately within the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), one must understand that, in the final analysis, phenomena do not transcend principle, nor does principle obstruct phenomena. When both phenomenon and principle are maintained together without neglecting either, only then can it be called "right contemplation" (*samyag-darśana*).

Be careful not to use this as a pretext to speak superficially and vaguely to later students; to mislead oneself and others is no small fault. Therefore, I have recorded this specifically as a warning.
*The Sutra on the Five Hundred Matters of Light and Heavy Precepts Spoken by the Buddha to Maudgalyāyana: A Brief Commentary*, Scroll Lower (End).

Phonetic Explanations: *Qiā* (cut by *qiū* and *jiā*). *Shè* (cut by *shī* and *zhí*; refers to insects that inject venom). *Jiàoxìng* (cut by *jiāo* [jīan yáo] and *xìng* [xià gěng]; "to hope for luck" means to covet what one ought not to obtain).
*Guànqìn* (*shè* cut by *shì* and *zhì*; *qìn* cut by *chū* and *guān*). *Hán* (cut by *hú* and *nán*; identical to *hán*).

The second page of the lower scroll contains more errors than the others (the character "合" in the seventh line is written as "令" in the Southern Canon). On the twentieth page, the character "角" in the fourth line is written as "捔" in the Southern Canon.

Phonetic Explanations: Bò (bó è qiè; to split). Sūn (pinyin: sùn; same as sàn; to spray). Tiáozhì (tiào tā diào qiè; zhì zhí zhī qiè; to leap and bound). Táng (tú láng qiè; to strike against or brush).

*Gòu-shú* (gòu pronounced as *jū-hòu*; to seek something by means of wealth; shú pronounced as *shén-yù*; to redeem a crime by means of wealth). *Yǎn-tàn* (yǎn pronounced as *yú-gǎn*; tàn pronounced as *tú-gǎn*; *yǎn-tàn* means black).
Lì (shénzhǐ qiè; to lick). Xiù (chījiù qiè; putrid odor). Lè (kūwù qiè; thick curd).
